CHAPTER 131
THE SHAPER

Hessa had removed the charcoal. Not from my arm. From the table. There was no charcoal stick beside the copper. No little marks waiting to become important. I noticed this before I sat down.

Hessa noticed me noticing.

“Good morning.”

“No target.”

“Good morning, Greg.”

“Good morning. No target.”

“Sit.”

I sat. Yesterday had left me with warm palms, a tired right calf, and the disturbing discovery that being called Person could require several attempts. This morning the palms were normal. Right calf normal.

Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present, mostly toes today. No pain. No thumb. No finger urge. Grip normal. Hessa checked twice anyway.

“You went back.”

I looked at her.

“Theatre.”

“Yes.”

“You were not a messenger.”

I narrowed my eyes.

“Teren's sister?”

“No.”

“Herb woman?”

“No.”

“Bread seller?”

Hessa wrote something.

“That is not an answer.”

“You are becoming easier to track than you think.”

“That sounds threatening.”

“It is mostly gossip.”

“Worse.”

She put the page aside. No more theatre. Good. She turned my right forearm palm-down on the support. Different position from last time. Not dramatically. Enough. I looked for charcoal again. Nothing.

“What question?”

“Direction first.”

I sat straighter.

“You think the prepared target pulled the response.”

“I think it may have.”

“So no prepared target.”

“Yes.”

“And you tell me direction before shape.”

“Yes.”

“That isolates whether changing direction after shaping was the problem.”

“No.”

I stopped.

“It helps distinguish it.”

“Yes.”

“That's what I meant.”

“No, it isn't.”

“Hessa.”

“Words matter when you are trying to decide what an observation excludes.”

“Fine.”

She pointed to a broad neutral patch on the outer half of my forearm. No mark. No suspended object. No thread. Her finger did not touch.

“Localized alteration in this region.”

“That is still a target.”

“A region.”

“A target region.”

“Yes.”

“So you did not remove targeting.”

“No.”

“You removed a fixed destination.”

“Yes.”

Better.

“What direction?”

“Toward your wrist.”

I looked at my wrist.

“Not elbowward.”

“Correct.”

“Why wrist?”

“Because your older unwanted pattern had a familiar elbowward component, and I do not want today's question tangled with it.”

“Good.”

“Also because you have a wrist.”

“That is less rigorous.”

“It is extremely well established.”

I almost laughed. Hessa did not. Probably on purpose. She reached for a narrow folded towel instead and slid it under my forearm. I watched her square the edges.

“You changed the support.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“The old one has charcoal on it.”

“That matters?”

“To the experiment? Probably not.”

“Then why mention it?”

“You asked.”

The towel raised my forearm perhaps half an inch. I flexed nothing. Still, the angle felt different enough that I noticed.

“Same arm position?”

“Close.”

“Close is not same.”

“No.”

“Does that become a confound?”

“Everything becomes a confound if you demand enough precision.”

“That sounds irresponsible.”

“It means I record it.”

She did. I looked at the page.

“You are writing towel.”

“Yes.”

“This is humiliating magic.”

“It is medicine with ambitions.”

That was worse. She moved the copper into view. Not close to the arm. Same familiar role. Observation. Not target.

“One draw?”

“Yes.”

“One shape?”

“Yes.”

“One directional instruction?”

“If the shape is stable.”

“RETURN.”

“Yes.”

“Release.”

“Yes.”

“No second trial.”

“Yes.”

“You decided that already.”

“Yes.”

“Even if it works?”

“Yes.”

“Even if it fails?”

“Yes.”

“Annoying.”

“Yes.”

She checked my hand position. Fingers relaxed. Wrist neutral. Elbow supported.

“Do not look at your wrist during the directional instruction.”

“Why?”

“I do not want you moving the hand or changing muscle tension while visually steering.”

“I wasn't going to.”

“Good.”

“Where do I look?”

“At the wall.”

I looked. Blank plaster. Excellent target.

“Before draw,” Hessa said, “tell me the full instruction.”

“Minimal draw. Localized alteration in the region you indicated. If stable, smallest asymmetry toward the wrist. No force. No broadening. Maintain underlying draw. Stop if anything changes outside the bounded response or if I cannot describe it.”

“RETURN on command.”

“Yes.”

“What direction?”

“Toward wrist.”

“Again.”

“Toward wrist.”

She waited. I waited. Nothing clever happened.

“Draw.”

I drew. Minimal. The copper changed. Right forearm. Familiar now. Not easy. Familiar. Those were different. No hand. No thumb. No left.

“Report.”

I did.

“Hold.”

Held.

“Shape in the indicated region.”

I shaped. The localized alteration appeared. Small. Not a point. Not a line. A patch with edges that were easier to describe than the center. It came slightly faster than last time. I reported that too.

“Stable?”

“I think.”

“Think or know?”

I waited. The patch did not broaden. No hand response. No movement.

“Know enough to continue.”

“Good. Direction.”

Toward wrist. I had known the direction before the draw. No charcoal. No fingers appearing afterward. No thread. Nothing to chase. I tried to let the smallest part of the altered edge favor the wrist side.

Something changed. I stopped doing anything more.

“Report.”

“Wrist-side edge sharpened.”

“Moved?”

“No.”

“Extended?”

“Maybe.”

“Maybe is allowed.”

“Center unchanged. Elbow-side edge unchanged. Wrist-side edge feels more distinct.”

“Anything else?”

“No.”

“Hand?”

“No.”

“Wrist?”

“No.”

“Thumb?”

“No.”

“Fingers?”

“No.”

“Left?”

“No.”

“Hold.”

I held. The wrist-side edge remained easier to find. Or I remained better at finding it because I expected it. That possibility arrived immediately. I told her.

“Good.”

“That was not good.”

“It was accurate reporting.”

“Possibly.”

“Still accurate.”

She watched my hand. I watched the wall. This was an absurd way to do magic. Probably healthy.

“RETURN.”

I returned. The localized alteration reduced. The wrist-side distinction softened with it. Underlying draw remained. No broadening. No motor urge. No wrist movement. No thumb. No unusual left response.

“Hold.”

Held.

“Release.”

Released. Hessa checked my hand before I could turn my arm over. Grip. Fingers. Thumb. Wrist. Temperature. Sensation. Fine. She wrote. I waited. She wrote more. I hated this part.

“Well?”

“You completed the sequence.”

“That is not the question.”

“It is one question.”

“The directional question.”

“Your report was consistent with a small directional asymmetry toward the instructed side.”

I stared at her.

“That sounds successful.”

“It sounds consistent.”

“Hessa.”

“You reported a sharper wrist-side edge. I did not independently observe the edge.”

“The copper?”

“Changed with draw and shaping. I saw nothing during the directional instruction that I would separate from that.”

“So still self-report.”

“Yes.”

“But unlike last time, it went the instructed direction.”

“By your report.”

“Yes.”

“Yes.”

I waited for more. She did not provide it.

“Does that increase your confidence?”

“In what?”

“That I can direct it.”

“A little.”

There. Small enough to be insulting. Real enough to matter.

“How little?”

“I am not giving you a number.”

“Qualitative scale.”

“No.”

“More than yesterday?”

“Yes.”

“Less than localized shaping?”

“Much less.”

“Less than RETURN?”

“Yes.”

“More than external effect?”

She looked at me.

“That is not a useful comparison.”

“Why?”

“Because one is an internal report about control and the other is a claim about effect outside the body.”

“Both are uncertain.”

“In different ways.”

Fine. I looked at the blank forearm. No charcoal. Nothing to point at afterward. The absence made the report feel less satisfying than Ch129. Then I realized that was backward. A mark had given me something visible to organize around.

Today Hessa had deliberately taken that away. I wanted to ask whether that made today's attempt harder. I asked.

“Possibly,” she said.

“Because there is less reference.”

“Possibly.”

“Could you mark the region after I shape instead of before?”

“Why?”

“So the mark cannot organize the initial response, but we still get a visual reference for where I reported it.”

Hessa considered that.

“Maybe.”

“Good idea?”

“Maybe.”

“You are abusing that word.”

“It is doing useful work.”

“What did removing the mark tell you?”

“Not enough yet.”

“It went toward the wrist.”

“Today.”

“You wanted direction first.”

“Yes.”

“And it worked better than changing direction after shape.”

“Today.”

“That distinction is becoming irritating.”

“It should remain irritating for a long time.”

“Do you think the charcoal caused the failure?”

“No.”

“You said it may have.”

“I still say it may have.”

“Then why no?”

“Because today's result does not tell me that it caused yesterday's result.”

“Ch129.”

“Yes.”

“Two days ago.”

“Yes.”

“Yesterday was theatre.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

She gave me a look. I had won something. Unclear what.

“Possible explanations,” I said.

“No list.”

“You hate lists.”

“I hate your lists before I finish my notes.”

“That is more specific.”

“Yes.”

I waited. She finished the line.

“Now?”

“No.”

“Hessa.”

“You already know them.”

“I want to know yours.”

“Fine. One: giving direction before shaping may help you organize the response.”

“Yes.”

“Two: removing the prepared charcoal destination may have mattered.”

“Yes.”

“Three: wristward may simply be easier than the direction I chose last time.”

I had not thought of that.

“Why?”

“I don't know.”

“Anatomy?”

“Possibly.”

“Old pattern?”

“Possibly.”

“Position?”

“Possibly.”

“Expectation?”

“Possibly.”

“You enjoy this.”

“No.”

“Liar.”

She continued.

“Four: your report may be biased by knowing the intended direction.”

“Yes.”

“Five: there may be a small real directional response that you can currently produce more reliably when the direction is established before shaping.”

I looked at her. She looked back.

“That one was last.”

“Yes.”

“You did that on purpose.”

“Yes.”

“Because it is least established.”

“Yes.”

I liked it anyway. That was my problem. I could already feel my attention trying to promote the fifth explanation because I liked it. The other four became obstacles instead of possibilities. I knew that habit.

Knowing it did not stop it.

“Hessa.”

“Yes?”

“If I had reported elbow-side instead, what would you have done?”

“Written elbow-side.”

“Would that lower your confidence?”

“In directional control under today's instruction, yes.”

“Would you think I followed some hidden prepared target?”

“There was no hidden prepared target.”

“Good.”

“Why good?”

“Because I was checking.”

She stared at me.

“You think I hid charcoal from you?”

“Not charcoal.”

“What?”

“I don't know. A scratch. A vein. Something you selected.”

“I selected a region of your arm.”

“So yes.”

“No.”

“Technically yes.”

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

She wrote again.

“What now?”

“Suspicious of clinician.”

“You did not write that.”

“No.”

I leaned enough to try to see. She covered the line with her hand. Rude.

“Repeat next assessment?”

“Maybe.”

“Same direction?”

“Maybe.”

“Opposite direction would be better.”

“Why?”

“Because if wristward is anatomically easier, opposite direction tests whether I can choose rather than merely produce a favored asymmetry.”

Hessa stopped writing. I waited.

“That is a reasonable question,” she said.

Excellent.

“So next time.”

“I said reasonable.”

“Hessa.”

“I did not say next.”

Cruel.

“What would be better?”

“I need to decide whether changing direction is worth another safe attempt before I have more ordinary repeatability at direction-first shaping.”

“So repeat wristward.”

“Maybe.”

“Then opposite.”

“Maybe.”

“Then external.”

“No.”

I had known that one. Worth trying.

“What about the thread?”

“No.”

“I did not ask to use it.”

“You were about to.”

“I was going to ask whether better directional control would be one of your reasons to reconsider it.”

Hessa paused.

“Yes.”

I waited.

“That is all?”

“That is all.”

“So if this becomes repeatable...”

“Then one reason to revisit an external question becomes stronger.”

“Not necessarily thread.”

“Correct.”

“Good.”

“Why good?”

“Because I am learning.”

She looked unconvinced. Fair. She checked my arm again. Still fine.

“What is the count?” I asked.

“Sixteen successful minimal draws.”

“Twelve shapes.”

“Yes.”

“Directional attempts?”

She paused.

“You are trying to create a category.”

“I am trying to count.”

“You have several attempts involving directional instruction under different conditions.”

“Four external REACH-type attempts?”

“Three external.”

“I know. I mean including internal.”

“No.”

I frowned.

“Why no?”

“Because you are about to make unlike things look alike by giving them one number.”

That was unfair. Also accurate.

“Ch129 changed direction after shaping.”

“Yes.”

“Today direction established before shaping.”

“Yes.”

“Both directional.”

“Yes.”

“So two internal directional questions.”

“If you want to write that in your notebook, you may.”

“Will you?”

“No.”

“What will you write?”

She turned the page slightly. Not enough for me to read all of it. Enough to see separate lines. Of course.

“Conditions,” she said.

“That is not a count.”

“Correct.”

I sat back. This was why she owned the room. Not because she was always right. She had been wrong before.

She had changed tests, changed language, shelved the thread after being interested enough to repeat it, and admitted when her own instruction might have been poor. That mattered more than pretending the sequence had been inevitable.

I preferred inevitable sequences. They were cleaner. Reality remained badly managed. Not because she was always right. Because she refused to let convenience become evidence when she could help it. I still wanted the number.

I would probably write one. Carefully.

“Tomorrow?”

She considered me. I hated when she did that.

“No magic.”

I blinked.

“Again?”

“Yes.”

“One day?”

“Yes.”

“Assessment after?”

“Yes.”

“Why rest after one clean internal attempt?”

“Because it remains an altered response in the same recovering system.”

“No symptoms.”

“Good.”

“Clean RETURN.”

“Good.”

“Clean release.”

“Good.”

“So why not tomorrow?”

“Because the absence of a problem is not a reason to increase frequency every time you notice the absence.”

I stared at her.

“That sounds prepared.”

“It is. You keep asking the same question.”

Fair.

“What am I allowed to do?”

“Live.”

“I know.”

“Apparently you need repetition.”

I looked toward the door. Theatre existed in that direction eventually. So did Lyssa, depending on where she was working. So did Sevren. So did the Guild. So did lunch. A surprisingly crowded category.

I had gone to theatre yesterday expecting one thing and been used as three other things instead. That thought belonged to yesterday. I left it there. Mostly.

What mattered now was that none of those places required me to know whether the wrist-side edge had been real. The fact was almost offensive. Carrow would continue functioning without a conclusion.

Hessa said:

“Greg.”

“Yes?”

“Do not spend tomorrow deciding whether today's wrist-side edge was real.”

“I cannot promise not to think.”

“I did not ask that.”

“What did you ask?”

“Do not turn the day into an unrecorded extension of this assessment.”

I considered arguing. Did not.

“Fine.”

“Good.”

I stood. My forearm looked completely normal. No charcoal to wash off. That was mildly unsatisfying. At the door I stopped.

“Hessa.”

“Yes?”

“If next time I produce the same wristward asymmetry again, does that count as replication?”

“It counts as another observation under similar conditions.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“It is the answer you are getting.”

I left. Outside, Carrow was already noisy. A cart blocked half the street. Two men were arguing about onions. Someone farther down was hammering metal badly. The bread seller saw me. I prepared for Messenger.

He said:

“Landlord.”

I stopped. He grinned. Absolutely fucking not. I pointed at him.

“No.”

He laughed hard enough to lean on the stall. I kept walking. Tomorrow, no magic. After that, Hessa again. Today the answer was not yes. It was not no either.

It was a sharper edge on the side I had been told to choose, observed by exactly one person from inside his own arm. Terrible evidence. Better than Ch129. I could live with that.
CHAPTER 132
THE SUITOR

I wanted to see Lyssa. Again. This was less annoying than the first time. Not unannoying. Less. No magic today. Hessa had been explicit. No draw. No shaping. No direction. No sitting at a table pretending I was not practicing.

Fine. I ate breakfast. The keeper looked at me.

“Landlord.”

I stopped chewing.

“No.”

She smiled.

“How?”

“Bread man.”

“I hate him.”

“You buy bread from him.”

“That can change.”

“It won't.”

Probably true. I left. Lyssa was not at the cloth market. Not at the bakery building from before. Not at the narrow shop where the older man had argued about red cord.

At the fourth place, a woman sorting bundles on a low cart looked at me and said:

“You're late.”

“For what?”

She pointed across the square. Lyssa was standing beneath an awning arguing with a man over a wooden crate. Not angry. Professional. Different. I crossed. Lyssa saw me. Her mouth changed. Small. Good.

“Gregory.”

“Lyssa.”

The crate man looked between us.

“Your landlord?”

I closed my eyes. Lyssa laughed.

“No.”

“Messenger?”

“No.”

Lyssa laughed harder. I looked at her.

“You know?”

“Apparently.”

“This city is diseased.”

The crate man said:

“I heard you forgot the letter.”

“I did not forget a real letter.”

“That is worse.”

“No.”

Lyssa touched my arm. Not helping.

“You came to find me?”

“Yes.”

She looked pleased. Also busy. Good.

“I have this.”

She pointed at the crate.

“What is it?”

“Not yours.”

“Correct.”

The crate man said:

“Glass.”

Lyssa looked at him. He shrugged.

“Now it's his.”

“No.”

“Still not mine,” I said.

“Thank you.”

Lyssa checked a folded scrap. Then the crate. Then the scrap again.

“Six?”

“Six.”

“You said five.”

“I said six.”

“You said five yesterday.”

“I wrote six.”

“Where?”

He pointed to the side. A charcoal six. Lyssa stared.

“That was not there yesterday.”

“It was.”

“No.”

I looked at the six. Then at Lyssa. Then at the man. Not my problem. Wonderful.

Lyssa said:

“Fine. Six. Same price.”

He said:

“More glass.”

“Your mistake.”

“Your order.”

“Your six.”

“Your glass.”

They continued. I stood nearby. Not adjudicating. Eventually Lyssa paid something. The man looked unhappy. Lyssa looked satisfied. Probably both had won enough. She took one side of the crate. I looked at the other.

“No.”

“I didn't say anything.”

“You leaned.”

This was everywhere now.

“I can help.”

“You have two crutches.”

“Yes.”

“And a crate full of glass.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

“Fine.”

The crate man called a boy from inside. The boy took the other side. Lyssa and the boy carried it twenty feet to a handcart. I followed. Useful. Very. The crate went onto the cart.

Lyssa checked the wheels.

“Where are you taking it?”

“Two streets.”

“I can walk two streets.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

She took the cart handles. I walked beside her. The cart rattled. Glass clicked inside. I wanted to know how it was packed. Did not ask. Progress. Probably.

“You're actually landlord now?” Lyssa asked.

“No.”

“That's disappointing.”

“I read six lines.”

“How many people did you evict?”

“None.”

“Bad landlord.”

“I was too loud.”

“Better.”

“No.”

She grinned. We crossed a narrow street. A wagon waited. Lyssa pulled the cart over the curb edge. One wheel stuck. I moved around.

“Push?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I have it.”

She rocked the cart once. Wheel cleared. Good. I kept walking. Two streets became three because the destination was around the back of a building. Lyssa stopped at a side door. Knocked. A woman opened it.

Looked at the crate.

“Six?”

Lyssa looked at me. I looked away.

The woman said:

“I ordered five.”

I laughed. Could not help it. Lyssa pointed at me.

“Don't.”

The crate man had been correct. Or Lyssa had been correct yesterday. Unclear. The woman checked her own paper. Five. Lyssa checked hers. Six.

“Why do you have six?”

“Because he had six.”

“That is not how orders work.”

“I know.”

The woman looked inside the crate.

“Keep six.”

Lyssa blinked.

“What?”

“I'll use it.”

“Same price?”

“No.”

Lyssa stared. The woman smiled. Negotiation began again. I sat on a low step because this was going to take time. Eventually the sixth piece stayed. More money changed hands. Lyssa came out.

“Everyone is difficult.”

“You are also everyone.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“Incorrect.”

She returned the handcart. Not to the crate man. Different place. I did not ask. She came back without it. A man waiting beside the cart place caught her before she reached me.

“Lyssa.”

She stopped. He held out a narrow wrapped parcel.

“Can you take this south?”

“When?”

“Now.”

“How far?”

“Dyer's row.”

She looked at the sun.

“No.”

He blinked.

“You're going south.”

“Not there.”

“It's on the way.”

“No.”

“It is almost on the way.”

“How much?”

He named a number. Lyssa shook her head. He raised it. She shook her head again.

“Tomorrow?”

“Maybe.”

“I need today.”

“Then you need someone else.”

He looked at me. I immediately hated that.

“Can he carry it?”

“No,” Lyssa and I said together.

The man frowned.

“It is light.”

“That isn't the problem,” I said.

Lyssa looked at me. Not annoyed. Maybe pleased. The man tried again.

“Double.”

Lyssa considered. For one second I thought she would take it. Then she looked toward the south street.

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I said yes to something else first.”

That was apparently the end. The man left with his parcel. I watched him go.

“You turned down double.”

“Yes.”

“You could have made it.”

“Maybe.”

“You had an hour.”

“I have less now.”

“You could move faster.”

Lyssa looked at my crutches. Then at me.

“That was not about you.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

She raised one eyebrow. Fine.

“I was calculating.”

“I know.”

“Your schedule.”

“Yes.”

“Not mine.”

“Exactly.”

That was annoying. Also fair.

“What was the first thing?”

“Work.”

“That is not detail.”

“You don't need detail.”

“I like detail.”

“I know.”

She started walking. I followed.

“Where are we going?”

“Leather stall.”

“Why?”

She held up one of the straps on her work bag. The stitching at the lower end had started to separate. I had not noticed.

“Repair.”

“You carry that every day?”

“Most.”

“How long has it been failing?”

“Today.”

“That did not happen today.”

“It became a problem today.”

Different standard. Fine. The leather stall was under a striped awning near a row of tool sellers. The man there took Lyssa's bag. Pulled the strap. Looked at the stitch.

“New strap.”

“Stitch.”

“New strap.”

“Stitch.”

“It will tear again.”

“Then stitch it again.”

He looked at her. She looked back. I stayed out of it. Mostly.

He said:

“Brown.”

Lyssa said:

“Black.”

“Brown matches.”

“Black is cheaper.”

He held up two strips. The brown did match. The black was ugly. Lyssa took black. I made a face. She saw.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You hate it.”

“It doesn't match.”

“It holds the bag.”

“Yes.”

“Then?”

I had been surrounded by theatre workers too long.

“Nothing.”

The leather man stitched the black strap reinforcement while we waited. Not replacing the whole strap. Compromise. Lyssa paid. She tested it by pulling hard. The leather man winced.

“Don't do that.”

“I need it to work.”

“It works.”

She pulled again. Still held.

“Good.”

We left. The black patch was visible from across the street. I hated it.

“What?” Lyssa asked.

“Nothing.”

“Still the strap?”

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“You're becoming decorative.”

“No.”

“Landlord.”

“Stop.”

“What now?” I asked.

“What are you doing?”

“Finding you.”

“You found me.”

“Yes.”

“So now what?”

I had not planned past that. Good.

“Food?”

“I have an hour.”

“Before?”

“Work.”

“Where?”

“South.”

“Can I come?”

She thought.

“No.”

Clean.

“Why?”

“Inside job. Stairs. Small room. Too many people already.”

“Fine.”

No apology. Better. She tilted her head.

“You okay with that?”

“Yes.”

“You made a face.”

“I have one face.”

“Apparently several people disagree.”

I hated everyone.

“Food.”

“Food.”

We bought meat pies from a stall near the fountain. Not the paper-bird square. Different fountain. Carrow had too many fountains. The pie seller knew Lyssa. Not well.

Enough to say:

“Late today.”

Lyssa said:

“Glass.”

The seller nodded as though that explained time. Apparently it did. He looked at me.

“Landlord?”

“No.”

Lyssa said:

“Yes.”

I looked at her. The seller handed me my pie.

“Rent's due.”

“I will burn this stall.”

“Then no pie.”

“Fine.”

I paid. Lyssa was still laughing when we reached the bench. We sat. Lyssa took the better side.

“That is mine.”

“You sat slowly.”

“I have crutches.”

“Excuses.”

I moved one crutch between my knees. The other leaned beside me. Not ideal. Stable enough. Lyssa bit into her pie.

“Did the magic do anything?”

I looked at her. She raised one eyebrow.

“You don't have to tell me.”

“It did something small.”

“Good?”

“Unclear.”

“That's your favorite.”

“It is not.”

“You say it a lot.”

“Hessa says it.”

“Then it's hers.”

“Fine.”

She waited. Did not ask again. Good. For almost a minute we ate without speaking. That should not have been notable. It was. Lyssa watched people crossing the square. A woman with three baskets.

A man carrying a chair upside down over one shoulder. Two children following a dog that clearly did not belong to them. I watched Lyssa. Not secretly enough. She looked over.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are staring.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I wanted to see you.”

That landed differently than I expected. Her expression softened. Not dramatic. Just less guarded.

“You found me.”

“Yes.”

“Again.”

“Yes.”

She looked back at the square. Then leaned her shoulder into mine once. Small. I liked it. I told her anyway.

“Thread is done.”

“Done?”

“For now.”

“Because?”

“It did not repeat cleanly.”

She nodded. No interpretation.

“Hessa tested direction instead.”

Lyssa chewed.

“What does that mean?”

“I was supposed to make a small change favor one side.”

“Did you?”

“Maybe.”

She pointed at me with the pie.

“Unclear.”

“Fuck you.”

She smiled.

Then:

“Are you allowed magic today?”

“No.”

“So don't.”

“I am not.”

“Good.”

That was the entire medical discussion. Excellent. She ate. A pigeon landed near our shoes. My phantom toes curled. Not actually. Sensation. Brief. Ordinary. I shifted my right foot instead. Lyssa noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You moved.”

“Pigeon.”

She looked down.

“It is not touching you.”

“It was considering it.”

The pigeon walked closer. Lyssa tore off a piece of crust. I stopped her.

“Don't reward it.”

“Why?”

“It has done nothing.”

“It's a pigeon.”

“Exactly.”

She fed it. Traitor. The pigeon ate. Then another arrived.

“See?”

“Friends.”

“Consequences.”

She fed that one too. Soon there were five.

“This is how institutions fail.”

Lyssa laughed so hard she almost dropped the pie. Good. We stayed. No purpose. The hour became forty minutes. Then thirty. Lyssa checked the sun. I noticed.

“You need to go.”

“Soon.”

“Now?”

“Not yet.”

She leaned back. Her shoulder touched mine. Stayed. I liked that. No analysis. Almost.

“You're going theatre after Hessa tomorrow?” she asked.

“I don't know.”

“Landlord duties.”

“No.”

“Messenger?”

“No.”

“Person?”

I looked at her.

“How do you know that?”

She smiled.

“No.”

“Lyssa.”

“No.”

“That one happened yesterday.”

“Yes.”

“Who told you?”

“People.”

“Which people?”

“Current people.”

That was deliberate. I stared. She laughed.

“You're awful.”

“You told me about the road.”

“I told you the road changed.”

“Yes.”

“You are using that against me.”

“Yes.”

“Unfair.”

“You were very serious.”

“It mattered.”

“So does Person.”

“No.”

“Did you have a line?”

“No.”

“Then what did you do?”

“Stood.”

She waited.

“And?”

“Moved.”

She waited.

“Badly.”

There. She smiled.

“Did you like it?”

I looked at the fountain.

“Yes.”

“More than landlord?”

“Different.”

“Messenger?”

“I forgot the letter once.”

“I know.”

“Everyone knows.”

“Yes.”

“This is humiliating.”

“You keep going back.”

“Yes.”

“So maybe humiliation isn't fatal.”

“I have extensive evidence.”

She laughed.

“Do you want a real part?”

I opened my mouth. Stopped. That was not a question anyone at the theatre had asked me.

“I don't know.”

“Good.”

“Why good?”

“Because you don't have one.”

“That is not logic.”

“It means you don't need to decide yet.”

I looked at her. She took another bite. No lesson. Just pie. Good.

“You like me.”

“Yes.”

There. Easy. I looked at her. She looked back. No joke. Not heavy either. Just true.

“I do.”

She nodded.

“Good.”

I kissed her. Short. Then again. Longer. The bench was badly designed for kissing someone while holding two crutches and protecting a meat pie. I moved the pie first. Priorities. Lyssa laughed against my mouth.

“What?”

“You saved the food.”

“Yes.”

“Romantic.”

“It cost money.”

“More romantic.”

I kissed her again. Her hand rested behind my neck. Mine on her side. Nothing dramatic. Good. A pigeon jumped onto the bench. I felt it before I saw it. Movement. Lyssa broke the kiss.

The pigeon stole crust from her paper. I pointed.

“Consequences.”

She stared at the bird.

“That was mine.”

“Yes.”

“Fuck.”

I laughed. The bird left. We watched it go. Lyssa checked the sun again. Now. She stood. I stayed seated. Before she left, a girl about twelve came running across the square.

“Lyssa.”

Lyssa turned. The girl held up a small folded paper packet.

“My mother said tomorrow.”

Lyssa took it. Checked the mark.

“Morning?”

The girl nodded.

“Tell her before midday.”

“She said afternoon.”

“Before midday.”

The girl shrugged in the universal way of people carrying messages they did not own.

“Fine.”

She ran off. I looked at the packet. Lyssa tucked it into her bag. Black repair patch visible.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You want to know.”

“Yes.”

“Tomorrow work.”

“Where?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because then you'll start planning my route.”

“That happened once.”

“It happened today.”

“With the crate.”

“With everything.”

“That is exaggerated.”

She kissed my forehead. Patronizing. Effective.

“South?”

“South?”

“Yes.”

“Inside?”

“Yes.”

“Stairs?”

“Yes.”

“Too many people?”

“Yes.”

“Fine.”

She looked at me.

“What are you doing?”

“Probably walking.”

“Strong plan.”

“I have a notebook.”

“Dangerous.”

She leaned down and kissed me once more. Then straightened.

“Tomorrow?”

There it was. Again. I looked at her.

“I have Hessa morning.”

“I know.”

“After?”

“Maybe.”

She rolled her eyes.

“You keep saying maybe.”

“You keep asking tomorrow.”

“Yes.”

Fair. I thought.

“I could find you after.”

“If I'm not there?”

“Then you aren't.”

“Good.”

That felt like an answer. Not appointment. Not promise. Just possible. Lyssa started south. I watched her go for maybe two seconds. Then stopped because staring became weird quickly. She turned anyway. Caught me.

“Landlord.”

“Fuck you.”

She walked away laughing. I sat another minute. My palms were warm but fine. Right calf ordinary. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present, heel against nothing. No magic. Good. I stood. The day was not finished.

I could go theatre. Guild. Home. Nothing. I chose nothing for a while. Walked without deciding. At one corner I passed the paper-bird seller. He recognized me. Held up a yellow bird. I looked at it.

The one on my table was yellow too.

“Not today,” I said.

He shrugged. No offense. Good. I kept walking. The thread did not enter my head. Not for several blocks. When it did, it was not first. Lyssa was. Annoyingly simple. Again.
CHAPTER 133
THE SHAPER

Hessa had removed the charcoal. Again. I liked that. Which probably meant I had developed opinions about blank forearms. Not ideal.

“Sit.”

I sat. Morning baseline was boring. Excellent. Hands normal. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present in the vague way it usually was when I thought about it and less present when I did not.

No thumb. No fingers trying to participate. No unusual cold. No pain. Hessa checked anyway. She always checked anyway. Then she put the folded white towel beneath my right forearm. Copper sat farther up the table.

Not near enough to be interesting. I looked around. No threads. Still.

“Disappointed?” Hessa asked.

“No.”

“You looked.”

“I have eyes.”

“Tragic.”

I rested my arm. The outer forearm was unmarked. No charcoal target. No line. No point. Nothing to accidentally obey. Good. Hessa sat across from me with her notes. She had rewritten something. I could tell because one strip of paper had been pasted over another.

“What did you change?”

“My wording.”

“Why?”

“Because I wrote that you directed the edge wristward.”

“That is what happened.”

“That is what you reported.”

I looked at her. She looked back.

“Fine.”

“Good.”

“I hate your notes.”

“They are not for your emotional comfort.”

“I know.”

She put the pen down.

“Last time I told you the direction before shaping.”

“Yes.”

“You reported a small asymmetry toward your wrist.”

“Yes.”

“Today I want the same sequence with one change.”

“Elbowward.”

She stared at me.

“That was my guess.”

“Stop guessing.”

“You said one change.”

“I did.”

“And opposite direction is the cleanest.”

“Probably.”

I smiled. She did not.

“Your confidence is unattractive.”

“That seems unrelated.”

“It isn't.”

I stopped smiling. Mostly. Hessa touched two fingers lightly to the table near my elbow. Not my arm. Just direction.

“Elbowward.”

“Yes.”

“Not toward my fingers.”

I frowned.

“You are indicating with your fingers.”

“I am indicating a direction. If I move my hand, the direction does not move with it.”

“Good.”

“You understand?”

“Yes.”

“Say it.”

“Toward my elbow. Not toward your hand.”

She moved her hand away. Good. No target. No destination. Only direction. That was cleaner. Probably. Hessa watched me.

“One draw.”

“One shape.”

“One directional instruction.”

“One RETURN.”

“One release.”

“Yes.”

“No external question.”

“Yes.”

“Do not make the effect larger just to make it easier to report.”

“I know.”

“Report what happens.”

I breathed. Not special breathing. Just enough to stop talking.

“Draw.”

I reached. Carefully. The draw came more easily than it had weeks ago. That did not mean easy. It meant familiar. A narrow opening. A small pull. Mana. Contained. No broad flood. No rush into the left.

No fingers. No thumb. No urge to move my hand. I held. Hessa watched my face more than my arm.

“Stable?”

“Yes.”

“Anything else?”

“No.”

“Hold.”

I held. The temptation was to prepare for the next instruction. I noticed that. Then I noticed that noticing it was also preparation. Annoying.

“Shape.”

Neutral region. Outer right forearm. Small. Localized. Not direction yet. That mattered. I let the familiar alteration form. Not a point. Not a patch exactly. An area with an edge I could feel more clearly than I could describe.

The center changed first. Then the boundary became legible. Not visible. Mine. Internal.

“Report.”

“Localized.”

“Size?”

“Small.”

“That is not size.”

“About the same as last time.”

“Comparison is not size.”

I almost opened my eyes. They were already open. I had been staring at the wall.

“Two fingers across. Maybe less.”

“Shape?”

“Uneven oval.”

“Already directional?”

I waited. Checked. Not pushed. Checked.

“No.”

“Certain?”

“No.”

“Useful.”

She wrote. I hated that too.

“Hold.”

I held. The edge stayed. No broadening. No elbow pull. No wrist pull. Nothing external. Copper remained copper. Wonderful object. Hessa waited long enough that I started wondering whether she had forgotten the next instruction.

She had not.

“Smallest directional change toward your elbow.”

I did not move. That was the first thing. No hand. No wrist. No fingers. No shoulder. Inside. Elbowward. The previous wristward attempt wanted to become relevant. I tried not to use it. Impossible.

Memory existed. Fine. I did not reverse it. There was nothing to reverse. This was a new shape. Elbowward. For several breaths nothing happened. Or nothing I could distinguish happened. I felt the center.

The wrist-side edge. The elbow-side edge. The elbow-side edge seemed softer than the wrist side. Wrong. Maybe. I waited. Hessa said nothing. I wanted to fix it. That was dangerous wording. Not fix. Observe.

Then the elbow-side boundary sharpened. A little. I thought. The wrist side stayed where it was. The center stayed. Elbow side clearer. Not farther. Clearer. Maybe.

“Report.”

“Elbow-side edge changed.”

“How?”

“Sharper.”

“Extension?”

“I don't know.”

“Other edges?”

“Wrist side same.”

“Center?”

“Same.”

“Anything else?”

“No.”

“Motor?”

“No.”

“Force?”

“No.”

“Broadening?”

“No.”

“Left?”

“No.”

“Hold.”

I held. The sharpened edge remained. Or my expectation of it remained. That was the problem. I knew what I was supposed to find. Hessa knew what I was supposed to find. The arm did not come with a second observer.

“Still?”

“Yes.”

“Same?”

“I think.”

“Think or know?”

“Think.”

“Good.”

She waited.

Then:

“RETURN.”

I reduced. The elbow-side distinction softened first. Then the rest. The localized alteration diminished without sliding. No familiar broad response. No hand urge. No thumb. No fingers. No wrist. No elbow movement. Underlying draw stayed.

“Report.”

“Reduced.”

“Gone?”

I checked.

“Maybe a little center.”

“Hold.”

I held. It faded.

“Now?”

“Gone.”

“Draw?”

“Still.”

“Release.”

I released. The draw closed. Nothing chased it. Nothing jumped left. Nothing moved outside me. Hessa waited. Then checked my hand. Forearm. Wrist. Thumb. Asked about fingers. Asked about phantom foot. Asked about the left.

All boring. Excellent. She sat back. I looked at the copper. It had contributed nothing. Also excellent.

“Well?”

“No.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is my answer to the answer you want.”

“What answer do I want?”

“That you can direct it.”

“I would accept that.”

“You would enjoy it.”

“Yes.”

“That is why I am saying no.”

I leaned back.

“So what happened?”

“You reported a small asymmetry toward the instructed elbow side under a direction-first condition with no prepared destination.”

“Yes.”

“That is the second time your report has favored the instructed side.”

“Opposite sides.”

“Yes.”

“So.”

“So my confidence increases.”

I waited. She did not continue.

“How much?”

“More than last time.”

“That is not a number.”

“I did that intentionally.”

“Can I direct it?”

“I am not writing that.”

“Can I probably direct it?”

“I am not writing that either.”

“What are you writing?”

She turned the page enough that I could read the line. REPORTED ASYMMETRY FOLLOWED OPPOSITE INSTRUCTED DIRECTION UNDER OTHERWISE SIMILAR DIRECTION-FIRST CONDITION.

Below it:

NO INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION. I read it twice.

“That is obnoxious.”

“It is accurate.”

“Yes.”

“That is usually why you dislike things.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

I looked at my arm. Nothing visible. Nothing externally measurable. Two reports. Two directions. Same problem. But not the same problem as before. That mattered. I wanted to do it again. Of course.

“Next time wrist again?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I have not decided.”

“We could alternate.”

“We could do many stupid things in orderly patterns.”

“That is unfair.”

“It is extremely fair.”

She closed the notes.

“One full no-magic day.”

I stared.

“Again?”

“Yes.”

“I am fine.”

“Yes.”

“That argument should eventually help me.”

“It does.”

“How?”

“You get one day instead of several.”

Annoying. Fair.

“Then next assessment?”

“Yes.”

“Direction?”

“Maybe.”

I narrowed my eyes. She noticed.

“What?”

“Everyone says maybe now.”

“Perhaps you are contagious.”

“That is worse.”

Hessa stood. Assessment over. I rolled my sleeve down. My forearm felt normal. My whole body felt normal. That should have been satisfying. It was. Also I wanted a third direction. There were not many useful directions on a forearm.

Wrist. Elbow. Up. Down. Inward. Outward. That was already too much thinking. Hessa waited until I finished my sleeve.

“Tomorrow is not an unrecorded assessment.”

“I know.”

“Say it.”

“Tomorrow is not an unrecorded assessment.”

“Good.”

I got my crutches.

At the door she said:

“Gregory.”

I turned.

“If you go to the theatre, do not decide that acting counts as neurological training.”

I stared at her.

“What?”

“The herb seller.”

“Oh, fuck all of you.”

Hessa smiled. Barely. I left. The bread seller was outside. I crossed the street before he could speak. He shouted anyway.

“LANDLORD.”

I kept going.

“MESSENGER.”

Better. I raised one crutch without turning. Probably rude. He laughed. I had no magic tomorrow. I had Hessa again after that. And I had two opposite directional reports that were not proof. Good.

I could live with that. For one day. Probably. I turned toward the theatre without deciding to. That was becoming a lie I told myself. Fine. I decided. The theatre doors were open. I heard voices before I reached them.

Not rehearsal voices. Argument voices. Better. Inside, the soot-shirt worker was standing onstage with a sword. Not a real sword. A prop. Long. Silver-painted. Ridiculous crossguard.

A red stone in the pommel large enough to purchase a small house if it had been real. The servant actor stood three paces away with both hands spread.

“It sounds stupid.”

“It is a sword,” the soot-shirt worker said.

“It is a legendary sword.”

“It is wood.”

“Onstage it is legendary.”

The recurring woman sat on the edge of the stage. Teren stood below with pages. Nobody noticed me for several seconds. I liked that. The servant actor pointed at the sword.

“It cannot sound like Teren.”

Teren looked offended.

“I do not sound like that.”

“You do.”

“I absolutely do not.”

The soot-shirt worker saw me. Her face changed. Danger.

“No.”

I said it immediately. She held the sword out.

“Gregory.”

“No.”

The recurring woman turned.

“Landlord.”

“No.”

Teren looked at his pages. Then at me. Then at the sword. I should have left. I did not.

“What?” I asked.

The servant actor grinned.

“The sword talks.”

I looked at the prop. Of course it did.

“Why?”

Everyone answered at once.

I caught:

“curse”

“king”

“third act”

“because it's funny”

and from Teren:

“Page forty-two.”

He held out the pages. I did not take them.

“What happened to whoever talks for it?”

“Nothing,” Teren said.

“He is standing right there,” the recurring woman said.

The servant actor pointed at himself.

“I hate doing both.”

“You have three lines,” Teren said.

“I hate all three.”

The soot-shirt worker extended the sword another inch toward me.

“Voice it.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“I am not a sword.”

The recurring woman smiled.

“You were a person.”

“That was broader.”

The servant actor laughed.

Teren said:

“Gregory.”

I looked at him.

“Read the lines.”

“From here?”

“From wherever.”

That was suspiciously permissive. I took the pages. Page forty-two. Three sword lines. Not many.

The first was:

YOU HAVE DRAWN ME, LITTLE KING. TRY NOT TO EMBARRASS US BOTH. I read it silently. Then again. The line was stupid. I liked it. No. The servant actor climbed onto the stage. He took the sword from the worker.

Held it in front of him.

“Start before.”

Teren pointed. The recurring woman stood. Another actor moved into place. Apparently we were doing this. I stayed below the stage. Seated would have been smarter. There was a chair. I took it. Good.

Teren started them. The servant actor crossed. The recurring woman said something about the sealed tomb. The servant actor drew the sword. Held it up. Everyone looked at me. I looked at the line.

“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”

Silence. The servant actor lowered the sword.

“That is Greg.”

“Yes,” I said.

“The sword cannot be Greg.”

“Then use someone else.”

The soot-shirt worker said:

“Again.”

I looked at her. She shrugged. Apparently everyone had learned Teren's word. The servant actor reset. They started again. Sword came out. I tried lower.

“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”

The recurring woman made a face.

“Now it is Greg pretending to be old.”

“I am old.”

Everyone looked at me. Fuck.

“Older.”

The servant actor laughed. Teren did not. He was listening.

“Again.”

Third time. I stared at the sword. Wood. Silver paint. Ridiculous red stone. Legendary. Supposedly. What did legendary sound like? Wrong question. What did this sword want? Also probably wrong. I had three lines.

The first insulted a king. Not loudly. Not angrily. It expected to be obeyed. I hated that I knew the difference.

“Again,” I said.

Teren looked at me.

Then:

“Again.”

The actors reset. The servant actor drew the sword. I waited half a beat longer than before. Not much. Enough that everyone was looking at the blade.

Then I said:

“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”

Different. The servant actor smiled. Not as himself. As the idiot king. The recurring woman looked at the sword. Not me. That was interesting. Teren tapped the page.

“Continue.”

I had forgotten there were more lines. Of course.

The king said:

“You know me?”

Sword:

“I knew better kings.”

I said it. Too fast.

Teren:

“Again from sword.”

“I knew better kings.”

The servant actor flinched. Small. Funny. The recurring woman laughed. Not audience laugh. Actor laugh. She covered it badly. The servant actor pointed the sword toward me.

“Fuck you.”

“That is not in the play.”

“It should be.”

The soot-shirt worker said:

“Keep it.”

Teren said:

“No.”

Everyone argued. I looked down at the third line. The sword apparently had opinions about doors. Of course. I wanted to read it. That was the problem. Not a large problem. A very small one.

Three lines. Wooden sword. No magic. No role. No casting. Nothing. I looked at Teren.

“Again?”

He smiled.

“Page forty-one.”

That was more than three lines. I opened to forty-one. The sword had been talking before it was drawn. From inside the scabbard. Ridiculous. Excellent. There were seven more lines before page forty-two. One complained about darkness.

One told the king his grip was embarrassing. One refused to answer a question because the king had asked it badly. I looked at Teren.

“Who wrote this?”

“Why?”

“It is rude.”

“Yes.”

“Constantly.”

“Yes.”

The servant actor said:

“You like it.”

“No.”

“You moved your chair.”

I looked down. I had. The recurring woman leaned toward the sword.

“Ask it something.”

“That is not how scripts work,” Teren said.

She ignored him.

“Oh, great blade, should Gregory be allowed near a stage?”

I looked at the sword. Then at her. Then back at the line in front of me. There was no answer for that. Good. I lowered my voice slightly.

“No.”

The servant actor folded over laughing. The recurring woman pointed at me.

“That one stays.”

Teren said:

“It absolutely does not.”

The soot-shirt worker said:

“Again.”

I was starting to understand how nothing ever got finished here. I moved the chair closer. Not onto the stage. Just closer. Tomorrow was no magic. Fine. Apparently I was a sword.
CHAPTER 134
THE VOICE

I was not going to the theatre for the sword. I was going because I went to the theatre. The sword happened to be there. This distinction mattered. Probably. No magic today. Hessa had made that very clear.

No draw. No shaping. No directional practice. No sitting at a table pretending I was merely thinking about direction. Fine. I ate breakfast.

The keeper said:

“Sword.”

I stopped.

“No.”

She looked pleased.

“How?”

“Bread man.”

“I am killing him.”

“You keep saying that.”

“One day.”

“Pay your rent first.”

“I am not a landlord.”

“Apparently sword now.”

I left. The bread seller saw me. Raised both hands. I crossed the street.

He shouted:

“BLADE.”

Worse. I kept going. The theatre doors were open. Inside, the sword was lying on a chair. Alone. That was offensive. It looked even more ridiculous without someone holding it. Wood. Silver paint. Huge red stone.

Crossguard like two knives trying to escape sideways. Legendary. Supposedly. I stopped beside it. The soot-shirt worker was crouched behind a painted wall tightening something.

Without looking:

“Don't touch.”

“I wasn't.”

“You leaned.”

Everyone had learned this.

“I was looking.”

“More dangerous.”

I sat in the chair beside the sword. Not its chair. Separate chair. Boundaries. Teren was sorting pages. The servant actor was onstage with the recurring woman and two others. Different scene. No sword.

Good. I watched. For maybe twelve minutes. Not waiting. Then the servant actor came offstage. Saw me. Saw the sword. Smiled.

“No.”

“You came for it.”

“No.”

“You sat beside it.”

“There were chairs.”

“There are many chairs.”

“This one had sightline.”

Teren looked up.

“No.”

“Fine.”

The servant actor picked up the sword. Held it vertically. The fake red stone caught light.

“Say something.”

“No.”

“Blade commands.”

“No.”

He pointed the sword at me.

“Speak.”

I looked at Teren.

Teren said:

“Page forty-one.”

Traitor. I took the pages.

The sword's first line from inside the scabbard:

IF YOU DROP ME AGAIN, I WILL ARRANGE FOR YOUR HEIRS TO BE STUPIDER THAN YOU. I read it silently. Good. Very good. The servant actor moved into position. He was playing the little king.

Not actually little. Younger than the recurring woman. Shorter than me. Most people were. He slid the sword halfway from the scabbard.

Teren said:

“From knock.”

The recurring woman knocked on an imaginary door. The king ignored it. Sword from inside scabbard.

I read:

“If you drop me again, I will arrange for your heirs to be stupider than you.”

Too normal. The servant actor looked at me.

“Greg.”

“Yes.”

“That is just you insulting me.”

“The line insults you.”

“The sword insults me.”

“That is what I did.”

“No.”

He put the sword back.

“Again.”

Teren did not say it. Interesting. They started. I tried deeper.

“If you drop me again, I will arrange for your heirs to be stupider than you.”

The servant actor stopped.

“No.”

“What?”

“I can't understand you.”

“I spoke clearly.”

“You spoke from a grave.”

“That seems appropriate.”

“Why?”

“Ancient sword.”

He held up the wood.

“It has been in a box.”

“Tomb.”

“Box.”

“Tomb in the play.”

“Box backstage.”

The recurring woman said:

“You sound constipated.”

I looked at her.

“Thank you.”

“Again.”

Third attempt. I removed some depth. Kept weight. Slower.

“If you drop me again, I will arrange for your heirs to be stupider than you.”

The servant actor waited.

Then:

“You took so long I forgot I dropped it.”

“That was one sentence.”

“It lasted a winter.”

The recurring woman nodded.

“Too grand.”

I looked at Teren.

He said:

“Again.”

Practical. Excellent. Fourth. No deep voice. No old voice. Less slow. But I tried to make every word precise.

“If you drop me again, I will arrange for your heirs to be stupider than you.”

The servant actor smiled. Then shrugged.

“Better.”

The recurring woman said:

“I looked at Gregory.”

Damn.

“Why?”

“You were doing the line.”

“The sword was doing the line.”

“No. You were.”

“How can you tell?”

She shrugged.

“I looked at you.”

That was not useful. It was extremely useful. I hated it.

“What changed last time?” I asked.

“Which?”

“Yesterday. When you looked at the sword.”

She thought.

“You waited.”

“That is timing.”

“Yes.”

“What else?”

“Nothing.”

“That cannot be true.”

“It can.”

The servant actor lifted the sword.

“You stopped trying so hard.”

“That is not measurable.”

“Neither is legendary.”

I looked at the sword. He looked at me.

“Again?”

“Yes.”

Good. We reset. Knock. King ignores it. Sword. I waited. Not long. Enough for the servant actor to glance down at the scabbard.

Then:

“If you drop me again, I will arrange for your heirs to be stupider than you.”

The servant actor's eyes stayed on the sword. Recurring woman watched the sword too. Better. But the line was less funny. Nobody laughed.

The servant actor continued:

“You cannot do that.”

Sword:

“I can barely imagine how I would make them worse, but I welcome the challenge.”

I read it with the same restrained weight. Still no laugh. Teren stopped.

“Too much.”

“What?”

“Too much sword.”

I stared.

“That sentence is impossible.”

“It isn't.”

The servant actor lowered the prop.

“You made it mean something.”

“It should mean something.”

“It means I dropped it.”

“It threatened your descendants.”

“Yes. Funny.”

“So the threat should be credible.”

“No.”

The recurring woman said:

“Credible enough.”

“That is meaningless.”

She pointed at the sword.

“Right now it sounds like it actually cursed six generations.”

“Yes.”

“So I don't laugh.”

“Why?”

“Because six generations are cursed.”

The servant actor nodded.

“I also stop being an idiot king and start wondering if I should put it down.”

“You should wonder that.”

“Not in this scene.”

Teren said:

“Again. Less.”

I sat back. Less what? Not voice. Not volume. Not speed. Less consequence. That sounded stupid. We ran it. This time I let the threat be casual. Almost bored.

“If you drop me again, I will arrange for your heirs to be stupider than you.”

The servant actor immediately said:

“You cannot do that.”

“I can barely imagine how I would make them worse, but I welcome the challenge.”

The recurring woman laughed. Servant actor fought a smile. Teren tapped the page.

“Keep.”

I looked at him.

“Keep what?”

“That.”

“That is not a note.”

“It is mine.”

“How do I repeat ‘that’?”

“Do it again.”

Of course. Again. I tried. It was worse. Too amused. The sword sounded pleased with its own joke.

Recurring woman said:

“No.”

“Why?”

“Now it knows it's funny.”

“The sword wrote the joke.”

“No.”

“Someone wrote the joke.”

“Exactly.”

I hated this conversation.

The servant actor said:

“Don't sell it.”

“What does that mean?”

“Say the insult. I will be offended.”

“That is division of labor.”

“Yes.”

Finally. Useful. Again. I said the line. He reacted. The laugh came from the recurring woman. Small. Good.

Teren:

“Next.”

I wanted to stay on it. Of course he moved on. The next sword line was from inside the scabbard. The king was arguing with a minister.

Sword interrupted:

HE IS LYING. Simple.

I read:

“He is lying.”

Too neutral.

Teren:

“Again.”

I tried ominous.

“He is lying.”

The servant actor looked down at the scabbard.

Recurring woman said:

“Too murder.”

“What does that mean?”

“It sounds like you're about to kill him.”

“The sword might.”

“Not here.”

Again. I tried contempt.

“He is lying.”

Servant actor looked at the minister. Better. Teren did not stop.

Minister:

“How would a sword know?”

Sword:

“Because you breathe differently when you lie.”

I liked that line. Too much. I gave it weight.

“Because you breathe differently when you lie.”

Teren:

“Less.”

I looked at him. He pointed at the king.

“He needs the line.”

What?

The servant actor said:

“You gave it to the room.”

“I spoke to the room.”

“You are talking to me.”

“The minister asked.”

“Yes. I am holding you.”

That was true. I looked at the sword. Then at him. Again. Minister asked. I answered toward the king. Not literally facing him. I was seated offstage. But I watched him instead of the page.

“Because you breathe differently when you lie.”

The servant actor reacted before the minister did. Tiny. A glance. Then minister answered. The scene continued. Teren stopped after three lines.

“Good.”

I looked down at the page. That felt different. Not bigger. Smaller. More specific. I wanted to know why. Dangerous. At break I took the sword. Not without permission. Soot-shirt worker handed it to me because I asked.

Progress. I weighed it. Light. Too light.

“It's wrong.”

She looked at me.

“What?”

“Balance.”

“No.”

“The pommel is huge.”

“Fake stone.”

“Yes.”

“The blade is wood.”

“Yes.”

“So?”

“It should feel heavier.”

“To who?”

“The king.”

She pointed at the servant actor, who was eating something near the stage.

“He knows.”

“That is not the same.”

“It is exactly the same.”

“The audience can see how he handles it.”

“Yes.”

“So if it is too light, he may move it too easily.”

She stared.

Then:

“Tell him.”

I did. Servant actor listened while chewing. Then lifted the sword one-handed. Twisted it. Flipped it around the grip. Caught it. I winced.

“That.”

“What?”

“You cannot do that with the sword.”

“I just did.”

“Legendary sword.”

“Wood.”

“Onstage legendary.”

He grinned. My own argument used against me. Fine.

“Hold it like it matters.”

“Why?”

“Because otherwise it looks like wood.”

He stopped chewing. Looked at me. Then at the sword. He took it again. This time two hands. Not because heavy. Because deliberate. He drew slower. The ridiculous prop looked different. Slightly. Damn.

He said:

“Like this?”

“Yes.”

He overdid it immediately. Shoulders rigid. Arms straining. Face solemn.

“No.”

“What?”

“Now it weighs a hundred pounds.”

“Legendary.”

“Fuck you.”

He laughed.

“Show me.”

“I cannot hold it and voice it from here.”

“Convenient.”

Soot-shirt worker took the sword. Held it naturally. No. Too normal. I pointed.

“Not that.”

She gave it back to servant actor.

“His problem.”

Good. We spent several minutes arguing about how heavy the fake sword should look. Nobody decided. Teren called us back. Apparently there were scenes. The next one was the draw from yesterday. Little king.

Sword.

“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”

I did it. Too prepared. Recurring woman looked at me.

“No.”

Again. I looked at the actor. He drew too casually. I stopped.

“No.”

He lowered the sword.

“What?”

“You ruined it.”

His face lit up.

“Oh, excellent.”

“You just pulled it out like a kitchen knife.”

“It is a sword.”

“Legendary sword.”

“Wood.”

“No.”

He laughed.

Teren said:

“Again.”

The servant actor drew it with too much ceremony. I waited. Too long. Everything became stupid.

Recurring woman said:

“You're both terrible.”

“Yes,” Teren said.

Again. This time servant actor drew it cleanly. Not casual. Not holy. Just with a little care. I waited until his eyes found the blade.

Then:

“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”

He looked offended. Good. The recurring woman looked at the sword. Good. Then servant actor said his next line too loudly. Bad. Scene fell apart. We laughed. Again. That became the afternoon. Not solving the sword.

Making it worse in new ways. I tried gravel. Bad. I tried age. Bad. I tried bored. Sometimes good. Too bored. Bad. I tried cruel. Killed the joke. I tried cheerful. Horrifying for unrelated reasons.

The servant actor tried holding the sword like it was fragile. Wrong. Like it was heavy. Wrong. Like he was afraid of it. Interesting for one scene, terrible for another. At one point he drew it, looked directly at me, and waited.

I stared back.

“What?”

“You're the sword.”

“Yes.”

“So talk.”

“You are looking at me.”

“Yes.”

“Don't.”

“Why?”

“Because then they look at me.”

The recurring woman, from across the stage:

“I did.”

Good. The servant actor turned his eyes to the blade. I delivered the line. The recurring woman kept looking at the blade. Better. Then he ruined it by nodding at the sword like it had just given excellent advice.

“No.”

“What now?”

“The sword did not say anything worth nodding at.”

“It insulted my bloodline.”

“Exactly.”

“How should I react?”

“Not like you agree.”

He pointed the sword at me.

“Then give me something else.”

“I gave you the line.”

“You gave me the same line.”

“That is literally my job.”

“No. Give me something I can use.”

I looked at Teren. He was enjoying this. Quietly. Traitor.

“Again,” Teren said.

We did. This time I made the insult drier. Not funny. Not cruel. Certain. The servant actor rolled his eyes at the sword. That worked. The recurring woman laughed. Small. He looked at me.

“See?”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“What did you do?”

“Something.”

“That is not useful.”

“Exactly.”

I hated acting. I loved acting. Teren cut one sword line entirely. I objected.

“Best line.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Scene is slow.”

“Then cut his line.”

Servant actor said:

“Traitor.”

Teren cut his too. Fair.

Later the recurring woman asked:

“What is the sword?”

I answered too quickly.

“Old.”

“No.”

“Legendary.”

“No.”

“Arrogant.”

“No.”

I looked at her.

“What answer do you want?”

“I asked what it is in this scene.”

I looked at the page. The king had just been insulted by a minister. Sword interrupted to make it worse.

“Unhelpful.”

She smiled.

“There.”

“That is not a character.”

“It is today.”

Then she left. I stared at the page. Unhelpful. The sword was ancient. Legendary. Probably powerful. Maybe cursed. It had seen better kings. It knew when people lied. It hated bad questions. And in that scene it was unhelpful.

That was somehow easier to play than legendary. I did not like that. I liked it a lot. By late afternoon my throat felt dry. Not hurt. Used. Teren gave me water before I asked.

I drank. The servant actor sat beside me on the stage edge. Sword across his knees.

“Better?”

I looked at it.

“Some.”

“Which?”

“I don't know.”

He nodded.

“That is acting.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

He laughed. Then held the sword up.

“What does it sound like?”

I thought. Not deep. Not old. Not always slow. Not always threatening. Sometimes bored. Sometimes cruel. Sometimes petty. Sometimes very sure it was the smartest thing in the room. That last one felt familiar.

Dangerous. I did not say it.

“It depends.”

He groaned.

“You've become Teren.”

“Fuck you.”

“Again.”

I laughed. My palms were warm when I left. Shoulders tired from the walk and crutches. Right calf tired. Residual limb quiet. No magic. Good. At home, the yellow paper bird still sat on the table.

I put my pages beside it. Teren had let me borrow pages forty-one through forty-three. Not take. Borrow. I read the sword lines again. Quietly. Not performing. Hessa had specifically prohibited directional practice. Nothing about swords.

Still, I stopped myself from saying them out loud. Not because magic. Because my throat was tired. Reasonable. I looked at the first line. IF YOU DROP ME AGAIN, I WILL ARRANGE FOR YOUR HEIRS TO BE STUPIDER THAN YOU.

The line was funny. The sword could make it not funny. The actor holding it could make it not legendary. I could make everyone look at me instead of the blade. Three separate ways to fail.

Probably more. Excellent. I turned the page. How do I make this better? That was a dangerous question. Good.
CHAPTER 135
THE REPEATER

My throat was normal. Hessa checked anyway. Not because of the sword. Because Hessa checked everything.

“Say ah.”

I stared at her.

“Why?”

“Because you said your throat was used yesterday.”

“It was acting.”

“Your throat does not care why.”

Fair. I said ah. She looked.

“Fine.”

“I knew that.”

“Yes.”

Palms normal. Shoulders mildly tired. Right calf normal enough. Residual limb quiet. Phantom heel present. Thumb quiet. Fingers quiet. No unusual left response. No pain. No cold. No numbness. No weakness. Boring. Excellent. Hessa placed the folded white towel under my right forearm.

No charcoal. No thread. No frame. Copper on the table. Same general position as before. I looked at it.

“Wrist?”

“No.”

“Elbow?”

“No.”

“New direction?”

“No.”

I frowned.

“You said no to all three useful options.”

“I said no to the three options you guessed.”

“That leaves many bad ones.”

“Yes.”

She opened her notes. Page from Ch131. Page from Ch133. I recognized the wording. Wristward. Elbowward. Self-reported asymmetry. No independent confirmation.

“You want replication,” I said.

“Yes.”

“Which?”

“Wristward.”

“Why not elbowward?”

“Because wristward was first.”

“That is not a reason.”

“It is enough of one.”

“No.”

She looked at me.

“Would you prefer I choose because I liked the result more?”

“No.”

“Then first is clean.”

Annoying. Fine. Same broad neutral outer-right-forearm region. No prepared destination. Direction given before shaping. Wristward. One attempt. No second attempt even if nothing happened. No external effect question. No thread. No casting. No Barrier.

No cleverness. I repeated the rules back. Hessa adjusted my forearm by less than an inch.

“Why?”

“Position.”

“It was fine.”

“It drifted.”

“It was comfortable.”

“That is not the same thing.”

She repositioned it. Fine.

“Direction?”

“Toward your wrist.”

“Not toward your fingers.”

“I am not indicating with my fingers today.”

She folded her hands. Good. Cleaner. Maybe.

“Draw.”

I did. Minimal. The draw established. Not instant. Familiar. That difference mattered. I held. No broadening. No hand. No thumb. No left. Hessa watched.

“Report.”

“Stable.”

“Anything unusual?”

“No.”

“Shape.”

I shaped. Localized. Small. Outer forearm. The center altered. Boundary formed. Not strongly. Enough. I waited.

“Report.”

“Localized. Maybe two fingers across.”

“Shape?”

“Oval.”

“Directional already?”

I checked. No. Maybe. I checked again.

“No.”

“Confident?”

“Moderate.”

“That is new.”

“What?”

“You used moderate.”

“I know degrees.”

“Rarely verbally.”

“Do you want the report or commentary?”

“Both.”

Of course.

“Hold.”

I held. The temptation was obvious. Wristward was coming. I knew it. My arm knew I knew it. That was not useful. Expectation problem again. But at least the direction was the same one we had already tried.

Replication was supposed to be contaminated by memory. That was part of replication. Probably. Hessa waited.

Then:

“Smallest directional change toward your wrist.”

I did nothing externally. Inside, I tried. Not force. Not shove. Not stretch. Direction. That word had become less clear the more often we used it. Toward wrist. At first nothing. Then the wrist-side edge seemed sharper.

Immediately. Too immediately. I distrusted it.

“Report.”

“Possible wrist-side sharpening.”

“Possible?”

“Too fast.”

“Does speed make it false?”

“No.”

“Then report sensation, not argument.”

“Wrist-side edge sharper.”

“Center?”

“Same.”

“Elbow side?”

“Same.”

“Extension?”

“No confidence.”

“Broadening?”

“No.”

“Motor?”

“No.”

“Force?”

“No.”

“Left?”

“No.”

“Hold.”

I held. The wrist edge remained sharper. Or remained expected. Same problem. I tried not to inspect too hard. That was impossible. Inspection was the task.

“Still?”

“Yes.”

“Same?”

“Yes.”

Hessa waited longer than I wanted.

Then:

“RETURN.”

I returned. The wrist-side edge softened. Center reduced. The whole alteration diminished. Underlying draw maintained. No hand. No thumb. No fingers. No wrist movement. No elbow response. No left.

“Residual?”

“Small center.”

“Hold.”

Held. It faded.

“Gone?”

“Yes.”

“Draw?”

“Still.”

“Release.”

Released. Clean. Hessa checked. Everything normal. Then she wrote. I waited. She kept writing.

“That repeated.”

She did not look up.

“Something repeated.”

“That is Hessa for yes.”

“No.”

“It followed wristward again.”

“Yes.”

“Under substantially similar conditions.”

“Yes.”

“No prepared target.”

“Yes.”

“Direction first.”

“Yes.”

“Same reported edge behavior.”

“Yes.”

“So.”

She put down the pen.

“So I am more confident than I was before.”

“How much?”

“Enough that I would now describe directional control as provisionally supported under this narrow condition.”

I stopped. That was more than I expected.

“Provisionally supported.”

“Yes.”

“Not established.”

“No.”

“Not freely chosen.”

“Not generally.”

“Not external.”

“No.”

“Not casting.”

“No.”

“Not Barrier.”

“No.”

I smiled. She did not.

“Can I have one good sentence without you ruining it?”

“You asked five questions.”

“Because you leave traps.”

“I leave boundaries.”

“Same architecture.”

“No.”

I looked at my arm. Provisionally supported. Narrow condition. Wristward. Direction-first. Internal report. No independent confirmation. Still. Better.

“What would establish it?”

“More replication. Another direction repeated. Better independent observation if we find one that does not distort the task. Stability over time.”

“Same wrist again?”

“Possibly.”

“Would that help?”

“If it repeats again under similar conditions, yes.”

“But still self-report.”

“Yes.”

“So eventually we need something outside my report.”

“Eventually I would like something outside your report.”

“Difference?”

“I will not spend unsafe attempts simply because independent confirmation is aesthetically satisfying.”

“That is not aesthetics.”

“It can become aesthetics very quickly.”

I looked at the copper. It had sat there through three directional assessments contributing almost nothing beyond familiarity.

“Could copper ever show direction?”

“Not with anything I trust from these attempts.”

“So stop looking at it.”

“I mostly have.”

“Then why keep it?”

“Because your draw response to it is familiar, and changing six conditions at once is how people invent stories.”

Fair. I hated how many useful sentences she owned.

“What if wristward is simply easier?”

“That remains possible.”

“Anatomically?”

“Possibly.”

“Then repeating wrist does not prove choice.”

“No.”

“Repeating elbow would help more.”

“Possibly.”

“Because it is opposite.”

“Yes.”

“So elbow next.”

“Maybe.”

I groaned. She smiled. Barely.

“I have not chosen the next assessment.”

“I know.”

“Then leave it there.”

“Fine.”

She closed the notes.

“One full no-magic day.”

I stared.

“Again.”

“Yes.”

“That is becoming insulting.”

“You recover well.”

“That sounds positive.”

“It is.”

She checked the notes from the last four assessments again. I could see the repeated words even upside down. LOCALIZED. RETURN. NO MOTOR. NO LEFT. The interesting words changed. The boring ones did not.

“What would make you give me two attempts in one day?”

“Reason.”

“I have reasons.”

“Medical reason.”

“Efficiency.”

“No.”

“Comparison.”

“Maybe.”

I looked at her.

“That was almost yes.”

“It was exactly maybe.”

“You enjoy this.”

“No.”

“You absolutely do.”

“I enjoy not injuring you.”

That was difficult to argue with without sounding deranged. I chose not to. Probably growth. Or fatigue.

“Does the rest day change the data?”

“It changes your body.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“It is the part I control.”

“And the interval between attempts?”

“Also recorded.”

“Could improvement just be recovery between attempts?”

“Possibly.”

“Could worse performance be fatigue from theatre?”

“Possibly.”

I stared.

“Everything is possibly.”

“No. Some things are no.”

“Casting?”

“No.”

“Barrier?”

“No.”

“External?”

“No.”

She had a point. I did not reward her for it.

“Then why no magic?”

“Because recovering well is not permission to remove recovery.”

I hated good sentences when they were used against me.

“Next assessment after?”

“Yes.”

“Directional?”

“I have not decided.”

“External?”

“No.”

That answer came quickly. I noticed.

“You decided that.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I do not yet need an external question.”

I waited. She elaborated because she was occasionally humane.

“You have just produced a third internally consistent directional report under a controlled sequence. That is exactly when I do not throw away the controlled sequence to chase something more dramatic.”

Fine. Good. Annoying.

“Can I say progress?”

“Yes.”

I looked at her. She looked back. That was almost suspiciously easy.

“Progress.”

“Yes.”

Good. I stood. She pointed.

“Pages.”

I froze.

“What pages?”

“The ones in your coat.”

I looked down. Sword pages. Forty-one through forty-three. Folded carefully inside my coat.

“How do you know?”

“Corner.”

A page corner had escaped. I pushed it in.

“They are theatre pages.”

“I assumed.”

“Not magic.”

“I did not say they were.”

“You looked judgmental.”

“I always look judgmental.”

True. She waved me out.

At the door:

“No magic tomorrow.”

“Yes.”

“No private directional rehearsal.”

“Yes.”

“No testing whether voice work changes anything in your arm.”

I turned slowly.

“What?”

“You have a face.”

“That is not a thing I was going to do.”

“Good.”

“That is insane.”

“Good.”

“Hessa.”

“Goodbye, Gregory.”

I left.

The bread seller called:

“SWORD.”

I ignored him.

Then:

“BLADE.”

Still ignored.

Then:

“LANDLORD.”

I turned.

“Pick one.”

He laughed. I hated him. The theatre doors were open. I had pages to return. That was why I went in. Obviously. The sword was onstage. The servant actor held it badly. I could tell from the doorway.

This was unfortunate. I crossed to my chair. Teren saw the pages in my hand.

“Returned?”

“Yes.”

He took them. Then gave them back.

“What?”

“Page forty-three.”

“You just took them.”

“Now I am giving them back.”

“This is inefficient.”

“Sit.”

I sat. The scene was already underway. Different scene. The sword had been awake for some time, apparently, and was speaking to the king while two soldiers tried to open a stone door. The servant actor looked at me.

Then deliberately looked at the blade. Good. He remembered. Teren pointed. Sword line. I read it the way I had yesterday. Dry. Controlled. Slightly bored. It sounded fake. Not terrible. Constructed. I heard the construction now.

The recurring woman, off to the side, said:

“No.”

I stopped.

“What?”

“You are doing Sword Voice.”

I hated the accuracy. The servant actor nodded.

“Yes.”

“That is the sword.”

“No. That is you doing the sword.”

I looked at Teren.

He said:

“Again.”

Of course. I tried less. Still Sword Voice. Less obvious. Still there.

The servant actor said:

“You are sitting differently too.”

“What?”

“You do this.”

He straightened, lowered his chin, and became an insulting imitation of me trying to be stately. The recurring woman laughed. I did not.

“Fuck you.”

“Accurate.”

“No.”

Teren:

“Again.”

I stared at the line. The sword was telling the king not to touch the door. Not because the door was dangerous. Because the king had already touched three things he had been told not to touch.

The line:

IF YOU PUT YOUR HAND ON THAT DOOR, I WILL PERSONALLY ASK THE DOOR TO BITE YOU. I had been making it legendary. Old. Certain. Above everyone. What if I did not? Not casual exactly.

Just spoke. Normally. That felt wrong. Good. I looked at the servant actor. He held the sword. Not reverently. Not carelessly. Just present.

I said:

“If you put your hand on that door, I will personally ask the door to bite you.”

My voice. Mostly. No depth. No added age. No deliberate weight. But something underneath changed without me planning it. A remembered cadence. Older. Not an old-man voice. Not gravel. Not theatrical age.

Just the way I had sometimes spoken when I had already explained something twice and someone was about to do the stupid thing anyway. Flat patience nearly gone. The servant actor stopped reaching toward the door.

Very slowly looked at the sword. The recurring woman laughed. Not huge. Immediate. Teren did not say anything. I looked at him. He lifted one finger. Continue.

The king said:

“You cannot speak to doors.”

I answered:

“I can speak to almost anything. Most things have better judgment than you.”

Same voice. Mine. But not nineteen. Not exactly. The sentence came out with an old irritation I had not used on purpose. The servant actor smiled despite himself. Then recovered. Soldier actor laughed. Teren stopped.

“Again.”

I blinked.

“What?”

“Again.”

“What was wrong?”

“Nothing.”

That was worse. I looked at the recurring woman.

She said:

“I looked at the sword.”

The servant actor said:

“I could play that.”

I looked at him.

“What was it?”

He shrugged.

“You.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“That was not me.”

“It was your mouth.”

“That is anatomy.”

“Again.”

I did. Worse. Too normal. Just Greg. The line flattened. The servant actor reached for the door too soon. Teren stopped.

“No.”

I laughed once. Of course. The good version had happened once. Again. I tried to remember the old cadence. Bad idea. Immediately became performance. Older. Too deliberate.

Recurring woman:

“No.”

“Fuck.”

Servant actor:

“Very legendary.”

“Fuck you.”

Again. I stopped trying to sound old. Stopped trying to sound like the sword. Looked at the actor. He put his hand near the door.

And I thought, with sudden perfect irritation:

Do not touch the fucking door. Then said the written line.

“If you put your hand on that door, I will personally ask the door to bite you.”

Closer. The servant actor froze. Recurring woman smiled.

Teren:

“Keep moving.”

The scene continued. I did not know what I had done. Good. Maybe. The next line failed. Then another worked. Then I rushed one. Then the servant actor held the sword too high and I told him so.

He told me to voice better. Normal. Excellent.

At break I asked the recurring woman:

“Did it sound old?”

She thought.

“No.”

“Older?”

“Maybe.”

“That is not useful.”

“It sounded like you already knew he was going to be stupid.”

I looked at her.

“That is specific.”

“Yes.”

“Did it sound nineteen?”

She stared.

“What does nineteen sound like?”

Fair. The servant actor came over.

“It sounded like the sword had dealt with kings before.”

I looked at him.

“That is in the text.”

“Yes.”

“So.”

“So it helped.”

“How?”

He shrugged.

“I believed you were tired of me.”

“I am tired of you.”

“Exactly.”

He walked away. I sat. The sword remained on the stage. Wood. Paint. Fake stone. No magic. I had spent yesterday trying to build a voice for something ancient. Today, for one line, I had mostly stopped.

And something older had shown up anyway. Not the sword. Me. That was strange. Not frightening. Just strange. I did not want to explain it. Not yet. Teren called us back. I stood halfway, remembered I was voicing from the chair, sat again.

Servant actor saw.

“Legendary.”

“Fuck you.”

He drew the sword. I looked at the page. No Sword Voice. No invented age. No gravel. No throne-room nonsense. Maybe. The problem was that I could hear the bad version now. That had not been true two days ago.

Two days ago deep sounded ancient because I wanted ancient. Slow sounded important because I wanted important. A lowered chin felt like authority because I had not yet watched everyone look straight at Gregory instead of the blade.

Now the failures announced themselves. Not before I made them. That would have been useful. After. Still useful. The servant actor shifted the sword in his hand. Not too casual. Not holy. He had changed too.

I hated that this was becoming shared. Which probably meant it was working. Teren lifted the page.

“Again.”

Fine. Again.
CHAPTER 136
THE VOICE ACTOR

I had made a mistake. Not with magic. Different category. The sword. Specifically, the voice. I had thought the useful thing yesterday had happened when I stopped performing. That was wrong. Or incomplete. The useful thing had happened when I stopped performing the wrong thing.

There was a difference. I realized this while eating eggs. Annoying. The keeper put bread beside my plate.

“Sword.”

“No.”

“Blade?”

“No.”

“Talking furniture?”

I looked at her.

“That is closer.”

He smiled. I ate. No magic today. Hessa had prohibited all of it. Fine. My forearm remained ordinary. Also fine. The problem was my voice. Not the one I had now. That one was easy.

Nineteen. Carrow. Crutches. Too much uncertainty packed into too many new things. My current voice did not sound young exactly. Not to me. It sounded normal. That was the problem. Normal had moved. The voice from before was not normal anymore.

I could remember it. That did not mean I could simply open my mouth and produce it. I finished breakfast. Walked to the theatre.

The bread seller shouted:

“YOUR MAJESTY.”

I ignored him.

“BLADE.”

Better. Still ignored him. Inside, the servant actor was already holding the sword. He looked at me.

“Late.”

“I am not scheduled.”
