“You keep saying that.”

“Because it remains true.”

Teren sat below the stage with pages. Recurring woman was pinning something to her sleeve. Soot-shirt worker had the sword's scabbard apart on a table. Not broken. Probably. I sat. The servant actor held up the prop.

“Page forty-three.”

I had thought about page forty-three while walking. Not rehearsed. Thought. Different. Probably.

The line:

SIT DOWN, IDIOT. Yesterday irritation had worked. Today I knew why. Or thought I knew why. That was dangerous. Teren pointed.

“From the stair line.”

They started. King hurt. Tries to stand. I breathed in. Wrong. Too much. I knew before I spoke.

“Sit down, idiot.”

Recurring woman looked at me.

Servant actor said:

“Sword Voice.”

“Fuck.”

Teren:

“Again.”

Reset. I tried less breath. Less preparation.

“Sit down, idiot.”

Flat. Dead.

Servant actor:

“Corpse sword.”

“Again.”

Third. I tried to find the thing from yesterday. The remembered cadence. Older me. Not old sounding. That was the trap. The man I had been had not gone around performing age. He had simply been older.

He had expected people to listen because, frequently, they had. He had known which arguments were worth having. He had been tired in ways nineteen-year-old me could remember but not naturally inhabit. He had breathed differently before speaking.

Not deeper. Later. There had been less hurry. Not because everything mattered more. Because fewer things did. I tried to put myself there. That took too long.

Teren:

“Gregory.”

“I know.”

“You missed it.”

The king was already standing. Damn. The servant actor lowered the sword.

“You disappeared.”

“I was preparing.”

“That is what disappearing is.”

Recurring woman:

“Listen.”

There. One word. Useful. Again. I did not prepare. I listened. The stair line. The king moved. His breath caught because the servant actor chose pain before standing. Different from yesterday. I heard it.

Then the weight shifted. Then the stupid attempt. The voice I wanted was not ready. Fine.

“Sit down, idiot.”

Current voice. Mostly. But I let the second word land after his movement instead of before it. The servant actor froze halfway up. Looked at the sword. Sat. Recurring woman continued. Teren did not stop.

Good.

After:

“Better,” servant actor said.

“It was not the voice.”

“No.”

“That bothers me.”

“Good.”

He reset. I stared at the page. The older voice had not appeared. But the scene worked. That was not enough. I wanted the voice. Of course I did. Next run I missed the cue again because I was trying to rebuild it.

Teren stopped.

“Gregory.”

“I know.”

“No, you don't.”

I looked at him. He tapped his ear.

“Listen.”

That was all. Everyone here had one-word religions. Again. I listened. Scene. Movement. Breath. Line. Current voice. Worked. Again. Worked worse. Again. Better. None sounded like before. At break I asked for water. Servant actor handed it over.

“You are doing a face.”

“What face?”

“Dead accountant.”

“I was never an accountant.”

“Then whoever you were.”

I stopped. He drank from his cup. I looked at him.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Gregory.”

“No.”

He waited. I hated that everyone had become good at waiting.

“I am trying to remember how I used to sound.”

He nodded like this made ordinary sense. Maybe for actors it did.

“Before what?”

“Before here.”

“Carrow?”

“Yes.”

True enough. He leaned back on his hands.

“What did you sound like?”

I opened my mouth. Nothing useful.

“Normal.”

He laughed.

“No.”

“That is the problem.”

“What?”

“It was normal then.”

“And now?”

“This is.”

I heard my current voice say it. Nineteen. Not high. Not childish. Just mine. Now. The old one had been mine too. That was the problem. Two normals. Only one automatic. Servant actor picked up the sword.

“Do it.”

“I cannot just do it.”

“You did once.”

“Accidentally.”

“Then accident again.”

“That is not how anything works.”

“Acting seems to.”

I looked at him. He grinned. Fuck him. I closed my eyes. Not dramatic. Just removing the stage. Old office. No. Wrong. Too specific. Old kitchen. No. Hospital corridor. No. Too much memory. The voice was not a place.

It was a whole arrangement. Breath. Attention. Expectation. How much time I thought I had. How much nonsense I was willing to tolerate. What I assumed about the person in front of me. How tired I was before the conversation even began.

How certain I was that I could leave if I wanted. The weight of decades that were not in this body. My shoulders changed. I noticed. Stopped. Too deliberate. Again. I breathed out. Let my chest settle.

Not older. Not deeper. Less forward. The servant actor was watching.

“That.”

“What?”

“You moved.”

“I know.”

“Do line.”

“No scene.”

He held the sword upright.

“Pretend.”

“No.”

“Coward.”

Fine. I looked at him. Not as servant actor. Not as friend. Not as idiot. As someone who had asked me the same avoidable question twice and was about to ask it a third time.

There. Tiny. Familiar. Unpleasant.

“Put the sword down.”

He did. Immediately. Then stared. I stared back.

Recurring woman, from behind us:

“That was different.”

I turned too fast. Gone. Completely.

“Fuck.”

She smiled.

“Again.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“I lost it.”

“Find it.”

Not helpful. Exactly helpful. I tried. Could not. I made my voice lower. Wrong. Slowed it. Wrong. Tried the face. Servant actor laughed.

“Dead accountant.”

“Fuck you.”

Gone. At least that was current me. Teren called break over. Page forty-one. Different scene. Comic threat. Great. I had not solved anything. Good. We ran it. First line too young. Not actually young.

Too immediate. The sword sounded like Greg insulting the king. Second attempt I manufactured oldness. Bad.

Recurring woman:

“You are wearing age.”

“What?”

“I can hear you wearing it.”

“That is not possible.”

“It is.”

Servant actor nodded.

“Very expensive age.”

“Fuck both of you.”

Teren:

“Again.”

I stopped trying to sound old. Instead I tried to rebuild the mental position. The king had dropped the sword. Again. The sword had warned him before. Probably. The line assumed repetition. That helped.

Not ancient. Not legendary. Tired of this specific idiot. I listened to the servant actor fumble the scabbard. He actually fumbled it. Not planned. The sword knocked against his knee. He hissed. Perfect. I did not hurry.

“If you drop me again, I will arrange for your heirs to be stupider than you.”

The servant actor looked at the sword. Not me. Recurring woman laughed.

Teren:

“Keep.”

I felt it. Not exact. Closer. The old cadence was there. But only because I had built the state under it. Breath first. Not a special breath. Permission to take the time. Then attention.

Not to the line. To the idiot. Then expectation. I did not need him to believe me. I assumed he would. That changed the line. I wanted to write this down. Dangerous.

Teren:

“Again.”

I tried to preserve it. Failed. Too controlled. The line came out polished.

Recurring woman:

“Gone.”

“Yes.”

“Again.”

This time I did not rebuild enough. Too current. Servant actor reacted late. Again. Too old. Again. Too amused. Again. Closer. Again. My throat started drying. Water. No heroics. I drank. The soot-shirt worker came over with the scabbard.

She had changed the inside lining.

“Try.”

Servant actor sheathed the sword. Draw. Less scrape. He drew again. Better. I watched.

“Why?”

“Sound was wrong.”

“What was wrong?”

“Too dry.”

“It is wood.”

“Yes.”

“Onstage legendary.”

She looked at me.

“You are becoming annoying.”

“Becoming?”

She left. Servant actor drew again. The cleaner sound changed his movement slightly. Less fighting the scabbard. The sword appeared more deliberate because the actor was not wrestling it. Interesting. Not my problem. Also absolutely my problem.

Teren called page forty-two. Draw scene. The line. Little king. I listened. The servant actor's new draw was smoother. He looked at the blade. I waited. Old state. Not old voice. The irritation was not right for this one.

This sword had just been awakened. It was not tired of him yet. Maybe disappointed in advance. That was different. I almost missed the line thinking that. Caught it.

“You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both.”

Good. Not great. Recurring woman looked at sword. Servant actor gave me something back. A small offended lift of the chin. The next line came easier. Not because the voice was ready. Because he was.

That mattered. We ran it again. Different. Still same sword? I did not know. That bothered me. At break I found Teren.

“What is consistent?”

He looked up.

“What?”

“The sword.”

“Yes.”

“What has to stay the same?”

He thought for maybe one second.

“Enough.”

I hated him.

“That is not an answer.”

“It is mine.”

“What is enough?”

He pointed to the stage.

“If I know who spoke before I look at the page.”

“That could just be the actor reacting.”

“Yes.”

“Or timing.”

“Yes.”

“Or the line.”

“Yes.”

“Then voice does not matter.”

“It matters.”

“How?”

“Gregory.”

“What?”

“Go do it.”

That was not an answer either. Fine. I went back. The servant actor had the sword balanced across his knees. He tapped the pommel.

“You're thinking too loud.”

“I am not speaking.”

“Exactly.”

“Fuck you.”

He smiled.

“Same sword.”

“What?”

“That.”

“Fuck you?”

“No. You.”

I stared. He shrugged.

“When you're trying to make it the sword, it changes too much.”

“So it should sound like me.”

“No.”

“Then what are you saying?”

“I don't know.”

Excellent. We were surrounded by professionals. Recurring woman joined us.

“He means stop replacing yourself.”

I looked at her. That was dangerously close to useful.

“I am nineteen.”

“Yes.”

“The sword is not.”

“Yes.”

“My normal voice is wrong.”

“Maybe.”

“It is.”

She shrugged.

“Then use something else.”

“I am trying.”

“I know.”

“Badly.”

“Yes.”

Servant actor laughed. I pointed at him.

“You too.”

“What did I do?”

“You keep changing how you hold it.”

“Because scenes change.”

“That is my point.”

“No, that is my point.”

We argued for five minutes. No winner. Good. Then Teren called us. Last run before lunch. Page forty-one into forty-two. Longer sequence. Several sword lines. Consistency problem. Perfect. I sat. Water. Pages. Servant actor ready.

I did not try to find old me before the scene. That was the change. I listened. Door knock. King ignores. Sword insults heirs. I let the old cadence arrive from the circumstance. Not all of it.

Enough. Next line. Different beat. Still same general presence. Then minister scene.

“He is lying.”

I almost made it ominous. Stopped. Listened. The minister had just overexplained. The sword did not need menace. It knew.

“He is lying.”

Servant actor glanced at blade. Minister challenged.

“Because you breathe differently when you lie.”

This line wanted certainty. Not age. Not irritation. Certainty. But the old normal had contained that too. Not magical certainty. Social certainty. The kind built from decades of watching people lie badly. I reached for that memory.

Too hard. The line delayed.

Teren:

“Gregory.”

Missed. Fuck. Again. I listened. This time I did not reach for decades. I let the actor's bad lie be enough.

“He is lying.”

Challenge.

“Because you breathe differently when you lie.”

Worked. Smaller. Cleaner. Recurring woman kept eyes on blade. Good. Then draw. Little king. I shifted mental state too late. The sword sounded annoyed instead of superior. Servant actor reacted as though scolded. Scene bent wrong.

Teren stopped.

“Again from draw.”

Again. Better. Again. Worse. Again. Better. By lunch I was exhausted in a strange way. Not physically much. Throat used. Brain tired. Holding the old state was work. Manufacturing it was more work. I could not simply become the man I remembered.

That man had existed in a body with different habits, different lungs, different assumptions, different years behind him. He had not needed to remember how long to wait before answering someone. He had waited because that was how he answered.

He had not placed his breath. His breath had arrived where decades had put it. He had not manufactured the weight behind a look.

People had already given it to him, one year and one argument and one responsibility at a time. I remembered the result. I did not own the process anymore. Now I had to build the result backward.

If I wanted the old pause, I had to choose not to fill it. If I wanted the old cadence, I had to hold my breath in a place that did not feel natural until the sentence had room.

If I wanted the old certainty, I had to put myself mentally above the immediate need to be believed. And if I tried too hard, all of it became visible. A nineteen-year-old boy wearing a dead man's posture.

Bad. Very bad. I had the memory. Not the automatic machinery. That distinction felt cruel. Also useful. I did not tell anyone. At lunch the servant actor dropped beside me.

“Old man tired?”

I looked at him. He froze. Then smiled slowly.

“There.”

I had done it by accident again. Or not accident. I was actually tired of him. Perfect condition.

“Fuck you,” I said.

Current voice. Gone. He laughed so hard he choked. Good. I drank water. No magic today. Tomorrow Hessa. Today sword. Both required more work than remembering how they were supposed to feel. I did not say that either.

The sword sat across from me on another chair. Wood. Silver paint. Red stone. Ridiculous. I looked at it.

“Same problem,” servant actor said.

“What?”

“You're staring at it like it owes you money.”

“It does.”

“How?”

“I have invested time.”

“That is not how swords work.”

“Apparently neither is anything else.”

He took another bite. I looked at the prop. The old voice was not hidden inside me. It was not a switch. It was a construction. Breath. Cadence. Attention. Expectation. Presence. Mental position.

And even if I built all of that correctly, the actor could change one beat and make the line need something else. Excellent. Terrible. I wanted another run.
CHAPTER 137
THE SHAPER

Hessa had paper. Too much paper. Not notes. Separate sheets. Blank. I stopped in the doorway.

“No.”

She looked up.

“What?”

“You have paper.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Sit.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the next event.”

I sat. Morning baseline first. Throat normal. Good. Hands normal. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom heel present if I looked for it. No thumb. No fingers. No wrist. No unusual left response.

No cold. No weakness. No pain. Hessa wrote all of that. Then slid one blank sheet closer. I looked at it.

“No magic drawing.”

“No.”

“Good.”

She put the sheet back.

“Today there is no direction.”

I looked at her.

“At all?”

“At all.”

“That seems regressive.”

“Yes.”

“You agree?”

“With the word you chose? No.”

“You just said yes.”

“I agreed it seems that way to you.”

Terrible woman. I rested my right forearm on the folded white towel. Same broad outer-forearm region. No charcoal. No thread. Copper farther up the table. No target. No indicated direction. Nothing.

“What is the question?” I asked.

“What does the localized shape do before we ask it to do anything else?”

I stared at my arm.

“That is boring.”

“Yes.”

“You are spending an attempt to characterize geometry.”

“Yes.”

“Not direction.”

“No.”

“Not external effect.”

“No.”

“Not progression.”

She looked at me.

“Gregory.”

“Fine.”

“One draw.”

“Yes.”

“One shape.”

“Yes.”

“Describe it at fixed points.”

I looked at the paper again.

“Then draw after?”

“Maybe.”

“You said maybe yesterday.”

“I say many things.”

“Structured self-report.”

“Yes.”

“Still not independent.”

“Yes.”

“Why paper?”

“To preserve your report with fewer words.”

“That sounds like drawing.”

“After release, if I decide the verbal report was stable enough to make the drawing worth doing.”

I thought.

“Why after release?”

“Because drawing during the attempt recruits the hand.”

Obviously. Good.

“Could I use the left?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because that is a stupid way to introduce a second motor task into an assessment about right-forearm sensation.”

Fair. She moved the paper away from me.

“Before draw, I am going to name four edges.”

“Wrist, elbow, upper, lower.”

“Yes.”

“Upper relative to what?”

“Your arm position now.”

“That is imprecise.”

“Useful enough.”

She pointed without touching. Wrist side. Elbow side. Upper side, away from the table edge. Lower side, toward the table edge. Not anatomical superior/inferior. Table geometry. Fine.

“At each checkpoint,” she said, “you report center and four edges.”

“That is a lot.”

“Yes.”

“You told me not to overreport.”

“I told you not to invent precision you do not have.”

Different.

“Do I report shape before size?”

“Whatever you can reliably distinguish first.”

“Could change.”

“Yes.”

“Useful.”

She smiled once. Barely. I had become infected.

“Draw.”

I did. Minimal. Narrow. Familiar. Not easy. Familiar. No hand. No thumb. No left. Stable.

“Report.”

“Minimal draw. No other response.”

“Hold.”

Held.

“Shape.”

No direction. That was harder now. Not physically. Mentally. I had spent several assessments waiting for an instruction to point the shape somewhere. Now there was none. I found the localized alteration. Center first.

Then boundary. Small. Uneven.

“Report when stable.”

I waited. The region settled.

“Center changed.”

“Yes.”

“Size around two fingers across. Maybe slightly longer along the arm.”

“Direction?”

“No instructed direction.”

“I asked what you perceive.”

I checked.

“Long axis maybe wrist-elbow.”

“How sure?”

“Moderate.”

“Edges.”

“Wrist side clearer than elbow.”

There. Again. Hessa did not react.

“Upper?”

“Softer.”

“Lower?”

“Clearer than upper.”

“Center?”

“Stable.”

“Shape?”

“Oval. Not symmetric.”

“Which edge most distinct?”

“Wrist.”

“Second?”

“Lower.”

“Elbow?”

“Third.”

“Upper?”

“Least.”

“How confident in that ordering?”

I waited.

“Wrist and upper, high. Middle two less.”

She wrote.

“Hold.”

I held. This was uncomfortable in the scientific sense. Not physically. I wanted direction. Not because I wanted magic. Because direction would give the asymmetry a reason. Without instruction, the shape was just asymmetric.

That was worse.

“Checkpoint two.”

I checked.

“Center stable.”

“Size?”

“Same.”

“Wrist edge?”

“Still strongest.”

“Elbow?”

“Maybe sharper than before.”

“Upper?”

“Still soft.”

“Lower?”

“Same.”

“Shape?”

“Oval. Maybe less uneven.”

“Maybe.”

“Yes.”

“Hold.”

Held. No broadening. No motor. No external sensation. Nothing dramatic. The shape existed. Or the report existed. Same old problem.

“Checkpoint three.”

I wanted the wrist edge to have changed. It had not.

“Center stable. Size same. Wrist strongest. Lower maybe second. Elbow close. Upper weakest.”

“Any spontaneous directional change?”

“No.”

“Any extension?”

“No.”

“Any drift?”

I checked.

“No.”

“Anything else?”

“No.”

Hessa wrote. Then waited. Longer. I looked at her.

“Are we done?”

“Not yet.”

“Why?”

“Time.”

“What about it?”

“I want one longer hold without direction.”

“That increases exposure.”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

“Short.”

“That is not a number.”

“Longer than the previous interval. Shorter than I would permit if this were perfectly boring.”

I smiled.

“Perfectly boring.”

“Do not make me regret phrasing.”

I held. The localized region stayed. Wrist edge still distinct. Then something changed. Small. Not magic outward. Inside. The upper edge sharpened slightly. I thought. I waited. It stayed.

“Hessa.”

“Report.”

“Upper edge clearer.”

“Compared to?”

“Before.”

“Wrist?”

“Still strongest.”

“Lower?”

“Same.”

“Elbow?”

“Same.”

“Center?”

“Stable.”

“Did you intend upper?”

“No.”

“Expect upper?”

“No.”

“Confidence?”

“Moderate.”

She wrote.

“Anything else?”

“No.”

“Hold.”

I held. The upper edge remained clearer. The shape was now more balanced. Still not symmetric. Maybe.

“RETURN.”

I reduced. Interesting. Which edge went first? I had not thought about that. The upper softened quickly. Then lower. Wrist stayed distinct longest. Elbow faded with center.

“Report.”

I did.

“Wrist persists longest?”

“Yes.”

“How sure?”

“Moderate.”

“Any movement?”

“No.”

“Any motor?”

“No.”

“Left?”

“No.”

“Hold.”

The region diminished.

“Gone?”

“Almost.”

Wait.

“Gone.”

“Draw?”

“Still.”

“Release.”

I released. Clean. Nothing chased it. No hand. No thumb. No fingers. No left. No external anything. Hessa checked everything. Normal. Then she put the blank paper in front of me.

“Now draw.”

I looked.

“With which hand?”

“Right.”

“That seems obvious now.”

“Yes.”

“From memory.”

“Yes.”

“Not exact anatomy.”

“No.”

“Just the shape.”

“Yes.”

I took the charcoal. Not magic. Ordinary. My right hand felt normal. I drew an oval. Stopped. Too smooth.

“That is wrong.”

“Then fix it.”

I flattened the wrist side slightly. Made upper edge softer. Lower edge a little more distinct. Then added a second faint outline for the later upper-edge sharpening. Hessa watched.

“Labels.”

I wrote:

WRIST STRONGEST UPPER SOFT, LATER CLEARER LOWER MODERATE ELBOW MODERATE CENTER STABLE I looked.

“That is ugly.”

“Yes.”

“Scientifically.”

“Yes.”

She took the charcoal.

Under the drawing she wrote:

POST-RELEASE STRUCTURED SELF-REPORT FROM MEMORY. NOT INDEPENDENT OBSERVATION. Good.

“You really enjoy ruining things.”

“I enjoy labeling them.”

“What does this tell you?”

“Several things.”

I waited. She did not continue.

“Hessa.”

“You want the directional answer.”

“Yes.”

“Today was not a directional test.”

“I know.”

“So I am not going to use it as one.”

I stared.

“Fine. What did today tell you?”

“That your neutral localized shape was not reported as symmetric.”

“Yes.”

“That the wrist-side boundary was the most consistently distinct edge across the observation period.”

“Yes.”

“That the upper edge changed without an instruction toward it.”

“Yes.”

“That your reported geometry changed slightly over time while the center and gross size remained stable.”

“Yes.”

“That RETURN was clean.”

“Yes.”

“And that a post-release drawing may be useful for preserving your self-report across sessions.”

I looked at the drawing.

“Useful enough to repeat?”

“Possibly.”

“Again tomorrow?”

“No.”

“One no-magic day.”

“Yes.”

“Then assessment.”

“Yes.”

“Neutral shape again?”

“I have not decided.”

“You absolutely have.”

“No.”

“What are your options?”

She considered.

“Repeat neutral shape.”

“Yes.”

“Repeat elbowward with a neutral pre-report first.”

“Yes.”

“Repeat wristward with a neutral pre-report first.”

“Yes.”

“Do neither and return to simple localization.”

“That seems less useful.”

“Possibly.”

“Could compare drawings.”

“Yes.”

“Could rotate arm position.”

“No.”

I stopped.

“Why?”

“Too many changes.”

Right.

“Same position first.”

“Probably.”

“Then later position.”

“Maybe.”

I leaned back.

“This is becoming geometry.”

“It was always geometry.”

I looked at her. She looked back. That sounded dangerously like theory. She did not expand. Good. I looked at my drawing again. Uneven oval. Not impressive. No glow. No thread movement. No object moving across a room.

A shape I could not see, drawn after it was gone. Progress. Maybe. I hated maybe.

“Can I keep the drawing?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Notes.”

“I made it.”

“During my assessment.”

“Communist.”

“What?”

“Nothing.”

She put the paper with the notes. I rolled my sleeve down. Throat normal. Arm normal. Everything normal. We had spent an hour proving that something invisible might be slightly lopsided. Excellent.

At the door Hessa said:

“Tomorrow no magic.”

“Yes.”

“No drawing it again.”

“I already drew it.”

“No redrawing from memory.”

“That is not magic.”

“It is assessment work.”

“You have become very broad about that.”

“Yes.”

“Fine.”

“No comparing the shape to your sword.”

I froze.

“What?”

She looked at me.

“The herb seller.”

I closed my eyes.

“Who told the herb seller about the sword?”

“Apparently everyone.”

“This city is evil.”

“No.”

“Small.”

“Not small.”

“Then explain this.”

“People talk.”

I left. The bread seller saw me. I pointed before he could speak.

“No.”

He opened his mouth anyway.

“OVAL.”

I stopped. He grinned.

“How?”

“Hessa buys bread.”

Of course she did. I considered murder. Did not. No magic tomorrow. The theatre was west. Lyssa might be south. Guild somewhere else. Home behind me. I stood at the corner longer than necessary.

Then went west. Not because of the sword. That lie had become unusable. Fine. I wanted another run.
CHAPTER 138
THE SHOPKEEPER

The theatre had become a warehouse while I was gone. Not metaphorically. There were boxes everywhere. A painted wall lay face-down across two benches. Three costumes hung from a rope where the alley usually was. Someone had stacked cups inside a helmet. The soot-shirt worker was on his knees wrapping the legendary sword in cloth. I stopped.

"No."

He looked up.

"What?"

"You are packing it."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Because we need it tonight."

I looked toward the stage. Teren was standing in the middle of it with pages in one hand and a piece of bread in the other.

"Tonight?"

He pointed the bread at me.

"Good. Sword."

"What is tonight?"

"Show."

I waited. He ate the bread.

"A show."

"Yes."

"Here?"

"No."

That was worse.

"Where?"

"East market hall."

"That is still Carrow."

"Yes."

"Why are you packing?"

"Because the market hall does not contain our scenery."

Reasonable. Annoying. The servant actor came through the side door wearing one boot and carrying the other.

"Gregory."

"What happened?"

"To what?"

"All of this."

"Thursday."

"It is Thursday?"

"I think."

Someone behind us said, "It is." The servant actor shrugged.

"Thursday."

I had apparently been attending theatre long enough to lose days and not long enough to know Thursdays were dangerous. A woman I had seen twice before crossed the stage with a red coat over one arm.

"Where's Meren?"

"Not coming," Teren said.

She stopped.

"What?"

"Not coming."

"He's in the second act."

"Not anymore."

She thought for perhaps two seconds.

"Who has Shopkeeper?"

Teren looked at me. I looked behind me. Nobody.

"No."

"Page twenty-six."

"I don't know page twenty-six."

"Excellent."

"That is not excellent."

The servant actor sat to put on his second boot.

"You're a shopkeeper."

"I am not."

"You look furious about money."

"That is not a profession."

"It is several professions."

Teren tossed me pages. I caught them badly against my chest because catching paper while using crutches remained stupid.

"Sit," he said.

"I am sitting for Sword."

"Sit somewhere else for Shopkeeper."

"How many roles am I doing?"

"Two."

"No."

"Probably."

"Probably is worse."

Teren had already turned away. I looked at the pages.

SHOPKEEPER.

Fourteen lines. Fourteen.

"That is not a small part."

The recurring woman passed me carrying a basket of fake vegetables.

"It is."

"Fourteen lines."

"Some are 'no.'"

"That still counts."

"Not emotionally."

I hated theatre. I sat. The scene was simple. A young man owed the shopkeeper money. The young man wanted more goods. The shopkeeper refused. The young man claimed his uncle would pay. The shopkeeper did not believe in the uncle. Then a constable entered. Then something about a goose. I read it again.

"Why is there a goose?"

Nobody answered. I read it a third time. The debtor's first line was an apology.

The shopkeeper's answer was:

YOU HAVE BEEN SORRY FOR ELEVEN DAYS.

That I understood.

The next:

IF I MUST COME OUT FROM BEHIND THIS COUNTER, THE PRICE INCREASES.

I looked at my crutches. Then at Teren.

"Teren."

"No."

"You don't know what I am asking."

"Yes."

"This line is stupid."

He looked.

"Why?"

I held up one crutch. He looked at it. Then at me.

"Fix it."

"What?"

"Fix it."

"You want me to rewrite it?"

"I want you to say something when he says his line."

"That is not the same thing."

"Correct."

The servant actor leaned over my shoulder.

"You expect me to move and grab your money?"

I looked at him. He smiled.

"That is terrible."

"You thought of something better."

"Yes."

"Then use yours."

"I haven't thought of it yet."

"Very Greg."

He left. I read the scene again. The actor playing the debtor was apparently the same man who had been arguing about belts two weeks ago. He arrived while I was still reading.

"You're Meren?"

"No."

"Good."

"What?"

"He spits."

"While speaking?"

"Sometimes."

"Why?"

"Teeth."

I stared. He had already moved on. Nobody was worried. That was the disturbing part. A person was missing. I had fourteen lines I had never performed. The market hall was somewhere else. The sword was wrapped in cloth. One actor had only just found both boots. And someone was painting a moon. Now. The show was tonight. Nobody was worried. I found Teren.

"What happens if this is bad?"

"The moon?"

"The show."

He considered.

"People don't like it."

"And?"

"And what?"

"Patrons."

"Some complain."

"Then?"

"Sometimes they don't come back."

"That matters."

"Yes."

"You seem unconcerned."

"We're busy."

"What if the entire show fails?"

He looked genuinely confused by the question.

"It has."

"And?"

"We did another one."

That was not enough. Apparently it was. The debtor actor appeared beside me.

"Shopkeeper."

"I have a name."

"Not tonight."

Fair. We ran the scene standing around a crate because the counter was already being carried outside. I sat behind it. He entered.

"Master, I come in humility and regret."

"You have been sorry for eleven days."

Too fast.

Teren, from somewhere:

"Again."

The debtor left. Returned.

"Master, I come in humility and regret."

I waited. Not old Greg. Not Sword. Just looked at him. He had the face of a man about to ask for something after announcing regret. I knew that face.

"You have been sorry for eleven days."

Better. He put both hands on the crate.

"And on the twelfth I will make you whole."

"No."

"That is not the line."

"It is now."

He grinned.

"Again."

We did it. He changed his apology. I changed no. He claimed his uncle had been delayed by rain. I asked whether the rain had also delayed his uncle's purse. That was not on the page. The recurring woman laughed from behind us. Teren said nothing. The debtor actor leaned closer.

"My uncle is a respected man."

"Then he will be embarrassed to learn you owe me money."

That was not on the page either.

"Keep moving," Teren said.

The debtor looked toward the imaginary door.

"I could simply leave."

There was a line.

IF YOU LEAVE, I WILL FOLLOW YOU TO YOUR HOUSE.

Stupid. I looked at my crutches. Then at him.

"You expect me to come over there and collect it?"

He stopped. I continued.

"No. Bring it here."

He glanced toward Teren. Teren made a small circular motion. Continue.

"And if I don't?"

I thought.

"Double."

The debtor laughed. Not acting.

"Double?"

"You made me consider standing."

The recurring woman barked a laugh. Someone dropped something behind the stage. The debtor pointed at my leg.

"You cannot charge a man because you are missing a foot."

I looked down.

"That sounds exactly like something a man who owes me money would say."

He lost the scene. Bent over laughing.

Teren:

"Again."

I smiled. That had felt different. Not old. Not young. Not manufactured. I knew what the shopkeeper wanted. Money. Everything else was obstruction. Easy. We ran it again. Worse. Of course. The double line came too early. The leg line sounded prepared because now it was. The debtor tried to feed me the same opening. I waited for the laugh that had happened before. There was no audience. Nothing. Teren stopped us.

"You're doing the last one."

"I know."

"Don't."

"I was trying to repeat it."

"I know."

"How do I repeat it without repeating it?"

He looked at me.

"Tonight."

Then walked away. Terrible answer. The market hall smelled like onions. That was my first impression. Second was that it was larger than the theatre and worse in almost every useful way. Low platform. Broad room. Support posts in terrible places. Doors on both sides. No proper wings. A rear curtain that moved whenever anyone opened the loading door. People were already coming in while we were still carrying things. I looked at the audience. Then at the stage. Then at Teren.

"They're here."

"Yes."

"We aren't ready."

"No."

"Why are they here?"

"Doors opened."

"Why?"

"Because it was time."

I hated all of them. The soot-shirt worker passed carrying a lamp.

"Move."

I moved. A painted doorway went up. The moon was still wet. Someone wiped paint off it with a sleeve and made it worse. The servant actor was now dressed as the king. I stared.

"You're the king?"

"Tonight."

"Who is carrying the sword?"

He pointed. The recurring woman. I looked at her. She had the sword.

"You're carrying it?"

"Tonight."

Everything was wrong. The sword was supposed to answer him. Not her. Different grip. Different height. Different timing. Different eyes. I found Teren.

"No."

"Yes."

"I rehearsed with him."

"Now rehearse once with her."

"We have people coming in."

"Yes."

"That is not rehearsal."

"Correct."

The recurring woman drew the sword. Cleaner than the servant actor. Too clean. I missed the line. She looked at me.

"Late."

"I know."

Again. No Teren. She resheathed. Drew.

I said:

"You have drawn me, little king. Try not to embarrass us both."

Wrong. She wasn't the king. She stared at me. I stared back. Then she smiled.

"Excellent."

"That line doesn't work."

"Then fix it."

"What is your character?"

"Tonight?"

"Yes."

"Princess."

"Why does the princess have the legendary sword?"

"She stole it."

"From whom?"

"King."

"Why?"

"Because he is an idiot."

That helped. A lot. She drew again. I waited until she looked at the blade.

"You stole me from a king and this was your plan?"

She smiled.

"What was wrong with my plan?"

"You are still here."

She laughed.

"That'll do."

Teren shouted:

"Places."

I had not finished panicking. Nobody cared. The show started. There was no Again. That was the first thing. A line landed badly. Gone. An actor entered too early. Now he was there. A cup rolled. Someone kicked it behind the counter. The moon leaned. Nobody died. The audience laughed in places I did not understand.

They did not laugh in places that had worked every rehearsal I had seen. The first scene dragged. I could feel it without knowing how. People shifted. A child talked. Someone near the back coughed for approximately a year. Then the servant actor entered as king and said something about taxes that was not on any page I had read. The room woke up. Not all of it. Enough. The actors moved faster after that. Nobody announced the change. They simply did. My Shopkeeper scene came before Sword. Good. Terrible.

The debtor entered. Different first line. Of course.

"Master, before you become unreasonable, I have an explanation."

The audience laughed slightly. I looked at him. He was waiting. I had a line. I did not use it.

"You've had eleven days to improve it."

More laughter. He put a hand to his chest.

"You wound me."

"No. Then you would owe me for the floor."

That got them. Oh. Not huge. But I felt it. The room gave something back. The debtor felt it too. His posture changed. Small. He leaned farther into being offended.

"My uncle will pay."

"Your uncle has become very expensive for a man I have never met."

He started toward the imaginary door. I knew what was coming.

"You're not going to follow me."

The old written line waited uselessly in my head. I looked at my crutches. Then at him.

"No."

The room laughed before I continued. Interesting. I waited. Not because Teren told me. Because the laugh occupied the space.

Then:

"That's why your debt doubles."

Bigger. The debtor stopped.

"Doubles?"

"You made me almost stand."

That hit harder than rehearsal. He pointed at my missing leg. I saw the line coming. He changed it.

"You have one foot. How expensive can standing be?"

Noise. Not laughter yet. Anticipation. I looked down. Then back at him.

"Would you like to lose one and compare?"

The room broke. Not everyone. Enough. The debtor stared at me. I had surprised him. Good. Then he smiled.

"Is that a threat?"

"No. Consultation."

More. I was good at this. That was dangerous. The constable entered late. Very late. The debtor and I both looked toward the door. Nothing.

The debtor whispered:

"Constable."

I said, louder:

"Apparently law enforcement has also decided not to stand."

The constable came through the wrong entrance laughing. The audience thought it belonged. Maybe it did now. The goose never appeared. Nobody mentioned it. After the scene I got behind the curtain and nearly walked directly into a painted wall. The servant actor caught my shoulder.

"Shopkeeper."

"That worked."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"No idea."

"Some of it was obvious."

"Good."

"I need to know which."

"Later. Sword."

Right. The sword was harder. Much harder. The recurring woman changed everything. She moved before lines where the servant actor held still. She looked at the sword less. She used it like something stolen rather than something inherited. My prepared tired familiarity did not fit. The first line got a small laugh. The second died. I tried to fix the third before she arrived at it. Missed her. She had already turned. I spoke to where she had been. Bad. She corrected without looking at me.

"Are you always this slow?"

Not on page. The audience laughed. I answered from behind the curtain:

"Only when carried by thieves."

Better. She lifted the sword.

"Then perhaps I should return you."

"To him?"

She looked toward the actor playing the king. The king was picking something off his sleeve. I waited.

"No."

Big laugh. The king looked offended.

"Excuse me?"

I had no line. The sword did. Apparently.

"You heard me."

That got another. Then the king improvised something too long and killed it. Completely. The room went quiet. He knew. I knew. Everyone knew. He finished anyway. The recurring woman looked at the sword. I could not save that. So I didn't. She moved on. Two scenes later an effect failed. A voice was supposed to come from behind a closed door. The actor backstage was not there. I knew because I was backstage. The onstage actor knocked. Nothing. Knocked again. Nothing. The soot-shirt worker hissed something obscene.

Then the servant actor, changing coats beside me, cupped a hand near his mouth and answered in a voice that seemed farther away than it should have. Not magic. Mostly. Maybe. The onstage actor continued. I looked at him.

"How?"

"Later."

"You threw it."

"Yes."

"From here?"

"Yes."

"That was you?"

"Yes."

"Do it again."

"No."

He pulled the second coat on.

"Show."

Right. The final act was better than the first. Not because the play improved. They did. Cuts happened without announcement. A scene I had watched in rehearsal lost nearly a third of its lines. A joke from the Shopkeeper scene came back when the king complained about taxes.

The servant actor, now somebody else entirely, looked toward where I sat behind the curtain and said:

"Careful. He charges double if he stands."

The audience remembered. They laughed before I did anything. I leaned around the curtain just enough for them to see one crutch. Nothing else. Bigger laugh. I disappeared. That was all. At the end people clapped. Some stood. Most did not. One man near the front looked annoyed. A woman beside him was laughing while she put on her coat. A child had fallen asleep. I could not classify it. Backstage, everyone started taking things apart immediately. I found Teren.

"Was that good?"

"Parts."

"That is not an answer."

"It is."

"The first act was bad."

"Yes."

"The king's long speech died."

"Yes."

"The Shopkeeper worked."

"Yes."

"The second Sword scene was better than the first."

"Yes."

"The door voice failed."

"Then didn't."

I looked toward the servant actor. He was carrying two coats and half a painted tree.

"He did that."

"Yes."

"How?"

Teren pointed at the tree.

"Carry."

"I cannot carry that."

"Then don't."

He pointed at a box of pages.

"Carry those."

I could hang the string around a crutch. Fine. I did. Outside, the troupe loaded the wagon under market lamps. Not our theatre wagon. A hired one. The soot-shirt worker was arguing about which flat went first. The recurring woman sat on the wagon edge eating something from paper. The servant actor threw a bundle up to her.

Someone said:

"Tomorrow we need the south-road wheels checked."

I looked over.

"Why?"

Nobody answered me. Then Teren did.

"Because we're leaving."

I stopped.

"Leaving Carrow?"

"Yes."

"When?"

"Two days."

"For how long?"

"Five, maybe six."

"Where?"

He named a town east of Carrow. I knew it. Not well. Old memory. A place with an old municipal hall whose roof had been rebuilt twice because the original load paths were strange and everyone kept blaming the stone. I had wanted to see it. Years ago. Decades ago. Different body. Different life. I looked at the wagon.

"The show goes?"

Teren looked at me like I was stupid.

"Yes."

"The sword?"

"Yes."

"Shopkeeper?"

"Depends who arrives."

I looked at my crutches. Road. Wagons. Loading. Unfamiliar stairs. Different rooms. People waiting. I did the arithmetic automatically.

"I'd be a hindrance."

The servant actor walked past carrying the wrapped sword.

"No."

I looked at him.

"Yes."

He lifted the bundle.

"You're the legendary sword."

"I voice the legendary sword."

"Yes."

"From a chair."

He nodded seriously.

"We have chairs in other towns."

The recurring woman called from the wagon:

"And shopkeepers."

"I am not a shopkeeper."

She laughed. Teren handed me another tied packet of pages.

"Tomorrow no magic?"

"Yes."

"Good."

"What does that have to do with anything?"

"Nothing."

He walked away. I looked at the packet. Then at the wagon. Then east. Five days. Maybe six. Not forever. The old hall was there. The show was there. Apparently the legendary sword was there. I wanted to go. That was becoming a problem. Good.
CHAPTER 139
THE SUBJECT

Hessa had moved the towel. I noticed before I sat down. Not far. Perhaps two fingers toward the end of the table. I put both crutches against the wall and looked at it. Hessa was grinding something in a small stone bowl. The room smelled bitter and green, with something sharper underneath that caught in the back of my nose. Morning light came through the narrow window beside her shelves and made every suspended bit of herb dust unnecessarily visible.

"You moved the towel."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"It was wet."

I looked at her. She kept grinding.

"You replaced it."

"Yes."

"In a different position."

"No."

"It is farther down the table."

Hessa stopped. She looked at the towel. Then at me. Then back at the towel.

"It is a towel, Gregory."

"That is not an answer."

"It is the only answer you are getting before you sit down."

I sat. The cot creaked under me. Hessa resumed grinding. I looked at the towel. Yesterday I had performed in front of an audience. Today I was suspicious of folded linen. This seemed like a decline.

"How was the show?" Hessa asked.

I looked at her.

"You know about the show?"

"I know you went."

"That is not the same thing."

"No."

She scraped the crushed leaves into a small paper fold. I waited. She did not ask again.

"Parts were good," I said.

"Mm."

"Parts were bad."

"Sounds like a show."

"You've been?"

"To shows?"

"Yes."

"No. I've spent my entire life avoiding rooms with chairs."

I frowned. Hessa glanced at me.

"That was a joke."

"I know."

"You looked injured."

"I was determining whether you were mocking Teren."

"I don't know Teren."

"Then probably not."

She put the paper fold aside and washed the pestle in a basin. Water tapped against stone. Somewhere below us, a door opened hard enough to rattle the window, followed by a man's voice complaining about somebody's cart. Carrow was awake. I had slept badly. Not because of magic. That distinction mattered. I had spent too much of the night remembering an audience laughing. Also not laughing. The not laughing had been more educational. Possibly. I had no idea. Then there was the trip. Five days. Maybe six. East. Temporary.

There was an old municipal hall there with a roof I had wanted to see before I died the first time. That was a perfectly legitimate reason to travel. The theatre was also going. Coincidence. Mostly.

"Sleep?" Hessa asked.

"Enough."

"How much?"

I told her.

"Water?"

"Yes."

"Food?"

"Yes."

"Alcohol?"

"No."

"Pain?"

"No."

"Cramping?"

"Ordinary."

"Residual limb?"

"Baseline."

"Right hand?"

"Normal."

"Forearm?"

"Normal."

"Phantom?"

"Ordinary."

She dried her hands.

"You said ordinary very quickly."

"It is ordinary."

"You checked?"

"No."

That was not entirely true. I had noticed. Noticing was not checking. Probably. Hessa watched me for another moment, then wrote something.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You wrote."

"I often do."

"What did you write?"

"That you answered too quickly."

"That contaminates the record."

"It is the record."

I disliked her profession. Hessa pulled the stool over and sat beside the cot. The copper strip was already on the small tray. So was charcoal, paper, and the same narrow measuring cord she had used before. No thread apparatus. Good. I had not expected it. I was still glad.

"What are we doing?"

"Drawing mana."

"Yes."

"Then shaping."

"Yes."

"Then reporting."

"Yes."

"And then?"

"We stop."

I stared at her.

"That is the entire assessment?"

"If nothing interesting happens."

"That is barely an assessment."

"You have become very difficult to impress."

"Nineteen draws."

"Yes."

"Fifteen shaping attempts."

"Yes."

"Three external attempts."

"Yes."

"And now we're going backward."

"No."

"We are doing something I could already do."

"That is not backward."

"It is not forward."

Hessa leaned over and tapped the paper with one finger.

"Last time you gave me a more detailed description of the neutral shape than you had before the directional tests."

"Yes."

"The neutral shape was not neutral in the way you assumed."

"I did not assume it was symmetrical."

"You drew it symmetrical."

"Because I thought it was."

"Excellent. We have located the assumption."

I shut my mouth. She continued.

"If your ordinary shaped state already has a more distinct wrist-side boundary, then a later report that the wrist-side boundary became more distinct under instruction means less than it would if the starting shape were even."

"It still changed."

"Perhaps."

"It did."

"You reported that it did."

I hated that sentence too. Hessa did not look pleased about saying it. That made it worse. She set my right forearm onto the folded towel. The position was familiar. Palm down, forearm supported, elbow free enough that I was not pressing hard into the table edge. I looked at the towel.

"It is different."

Hessa closed her eyes.

"Gregory."

"Two fingers."

"You may leave."

"I didn't say it invalidated the test."

"You are looking at cloth instead of your arm."

"I can do both."

"That is precisely the problem."

Fair. I looked at my arm. Hessa adjusted the copper strip.

"Minimal draw."

I breathed. Reached. Mana came. Not dramatically. It had stopped feeling dramatic several assessments ago, which was probably dangerous in its own way. There. Present. Contained. The copper responded.

"Confirmed," Hessa said.

I held. Right side normal. Hand normal. Thumb quiet. No motor urge. No cold. No pain. My left phantom foot existed somewhere below the cot, vague and familiar and completely uninvolved.

"Shape," Hessa said.

I formed the small alteration in the right forearm. No direction. No external reach. Just the shape. It gathered slowly enough that I could feel the temptation to help it. I did not. There.

"Hold."

I held.

"Report."

"Localized. Similar size to last time."

"Similar is interpretation. Edges."

Right. I closed my eyes. Not because I needed to. Because the room became less annoying.

"Wrist-side boundary is clearest."

Hessa said nothing.

"Upper edge less distinct. Elbow side softer. Lower edge..."

I waited.

"Lower edge is difficult."

"Meaning?"

"I can tell where I think it stops. I cannot tell whether I'm feeling the end of the shape or the point where my attention stops being useful."

"Good."

"That wasn't a success."

"It was a report."

Fine.

"Anything changing?"

I waited. The shape stayed. Or mostly stayed. The upper edge felt broader than it had at the start. I did not like that.

"Upper edge may be spreading."

"May?"

"Yes."

"Direction?"

"Not instructed."

"I asked what direction."

"Oh. Toward the outside of the forearm. Slightly."

"Other edges?"

"Wrist side still clearest. Elbow side soft. Lower unclear."

Hessa wrote. I could hear the charcoal moving. Scritch. Pause. Scritch. It was surprisingly irritating.

"Draw it," she said.

"With my left hand?"

"Yes."

"My left hand draws badly."

"It drew badly last time."

"So we are preserving the variable."

"Yes."

I opened my eyes. Hessa put the paper where I could reach it without moving my right forearm. I took the charcoal in my left hand. The first line looked like a potato.

"This is useless."

"Continue."

I drew the wrist-side edge darker. Then the upper edge. Then the softer elbow side. The lower boundary got a broken line because I did not trust it. Hessa watched the paper, not my face.

"Done?"

"Yes."

"Look at the prior one."

She turned over a sheet beside her ledger. My drawing from the last assessment. I looked between them. Oh. The wrist-side boundary was dark in both. The elbow side was soft in both. The upper edge was not identical, but it was close enough that I could not dismiss it as nothing. The lower edge on the old drawing had been cleaner. Or I had drawn it cleaner. Those were not the same fact.

"Again," I said.

"No."

"One more neutral shape."

"No."

"Same setup."

"No."

"Why?"

"Because you are already comparing."

"That is the point."

"Not while you are holding mana."

I looked at my right arm. Fuck.

"Return," Hessa said.

I reduced the shape. The wrist-side edge softened first. Again. Not completely. The center faded. Upper edge lingered. I continued the same return without separately correcting it.

"Report."

"Wrist side reduced. Center reduced. Upper edge remains clearer."

"Continue."

I did. The remaining edge softened. Then I reached the familiar ugly point where I could not tell whether something remained or whether I was searching for it because Hessa had asked me to.

"Uncertain."

"Hold draw."

I held the underlying mana. The shaped alteration was either gone or below my confidence.

"Copper?"

"Draw remains," Hessa said.

"Release."

I released. The mana went. Nothing jumped. Nothing hurt. Nothing moved outside me. No thread trembled. No revelation occurred. Hessa waited anyway. She checked my hand, wrist, forearm, breathing, residual limb, and the things she always checked even when I was increasingly convinced she could do half of it by glaring.

"Anything?"

"No."

"Stand."

I reached for the crutches. She watched me rise. Right foot planted. Hands loaded. Hips came forward. Normal. I settled.

"Anything?"

"No."

"Walk."

I went to the window and back. The room was not large enough to make this dignified.

"Anything?"

"My dignity is declining."

"Baseline."

I looked at her. She wrote it down.

"You did not."

"I did."

"Hessa."

She smiled without looking up. Barely. That was worse than laughter. I sat again. She put the two drawings side by side. They were not identical. They were also not very different. I leaned closer.

"If that's the ordinary geometry," I said, "then the directional tests are weaker."

"Yes."

"Not gone."

"No."

"Because there were changes after instruction."

"Reported changes."

"Yes, yes."

"And because the prior tests were not mapped this way before the instruction, we cannot compare their starting geometry at the same level of detail."

I stared at the pages. That annoyed me more than if she had simply said the tests were bad. Bad could be discarded. These were not bad. They were incomplete. Much worse.

"So we repeat them."

"Eventually."

"With a pre-map."

"Possibly."

"Same position."

"Possibly."

"Same towel."

Hessa looked at me.

"I will preserve the sacred towel."

"Thank you."

"I'll label it."

"That would actually help."

"I regret speaking."

She stacked the papers. I watched her. There was still something missing.

"What did today establish?"

"Establish is too strong."

"Fine. What did today support?"

"That your neutral shaped state may have a repeatable asymmetry under this setup."

"May."

"Yes."

"Wrist-side boundary more distinct."

"In two detailed reports."

"And upper edge changes without directional instruction."

"In both assessments, though not identically."

"So anatomy?"

"Maybe."

"Support pressure?"

"Maybe."

"Arm position?"

"Maybe."

"Natural magical geometry?"

"Maybe."

"Expectation?"

"Maybe."

"Day variation?"

"Maybe."

I sighed.

"You really do have one answer."

"I have several. You keep asking questions with the same answer."

I looked at the two drawings again. Then I remembered the wagon. Not because it had anything to do with my forearm. Because it was leaving. Tomorrow, apparently. I had known that before coming here. I had not intended to bring it up until after the assessment. That was sensible. The assessment was medical and magical. The theatre was theatre. Separate.

"Hessa."

"No."

"I haven't asked."

"You changed your voice."

I stared at her.

"What does that mean?"

"You have an administrative question."

"I do not have an administrative voice."

"You absolutely do."

I considered objecting. That would delay the question.

"The theatre is leaving Carrow tomorrow."

Hessa's hand stopped over the ledger.

"For how long?"

"Five days. Maybe six."

"Where?"

I told her. She knew the town. Of course she did. Hessa knew every place within a week's travel where somebody had once broken a wrist badly.

"Why are you telling me?"

"Because I might go."

"Might?"

"Yes."

She waited. I disliked silence when other people used it deliberately.

"I want to see the municipal hall," I said.

Hessa nodded.

"The roof was rebuilt twice."

"Mm."

"The original load paths are strange."

"I'm sure."

"And the theatre is performing there."

"An extraordinary coincidence."

I looked at her. She remained completely serious.

"I would be traveling with them."

"Yes."

"There would be wagons."

"I know what theatres use."

"Do you?"

"No. But I know what roads use."

Fair.

"I wouldn't test anything independently."

"No."

"I wouldn't draw."

"No."

"I wouldn't shape."

"No."

"I wouldn't cast."

"No."

"I know."

"I am enjoying this part."

I shifted on the cot.

"What I am asking is whether going changes your restrictions."

"Yes."

My stomach tightened. Hessa closed the ledger.

"You will be somewhere else."

"That is not what I meant."

"It is what I mean. If you are injured, sick, exhausted, or develop a new symptom, I am not there."

"I understand."

"Do you?"

"Yes."

"You said you slept enough this morning."

"I did."

"You slept badly."

I stopped. She had not asked whether I slept well. Only how much. Annoying woman.

"I slept enough badly."

"That sentence is why I worry about you."

"You don't worry about me."

"No."

She began wrapping the charcoal in cloth.

"I simply arrange my professional decisions around the possibility that you will do something stupid."

"That sounds like worry."

"It is risk management."

She tied the cloth twice. Too tightly for something she did not care about. I did not mention it.

"So can I go?"

"I don't control where you travel."

"That is evasive."

"It is accurate. I control what magical work I supervise and what I clear you to do."

"And?"

"And you remain uncleared for independent draw, shaping, casting, Barrier work, external testing, or whatever clever category you invent because you think it isn't technically one of those."

"I wasn't going to."

Hessa looked at me.

"I wasn't."

She kept looking.

"I probably wasn't."

"Better."

I rubbed my palm against my trouser leg.

"If I go, when is the next assessment?"

"When you return."

"That could be six days."

"Yes."

"We've been working on a shorter cadence."

"Yes."

"So the gap changes the sequence."

"Yes."

I waited. Hessa waited back.

"You're not going to tell me not to go."

"No."

"Why?"

"Do you want me to?"

"No."

"Then this is an odd complaint."

"I expected you to object."

"I object to unsupervised magic. I object to you converting uncertainty into permission. I object to you pretending symptoms don't count because they interfere with your plans."

"I don't do that."

She looked at me. Fine.

"Not consistently."

"Better."

She stood and carried the bowl to the shelf. I looked at the drawings again. Six days without an assessment. Possibly. Five. The theatre had chairs in other towns. Apparently. Also shopkeepers. I could stay. That would be easier. Known room. Known stairs. Hessa. Guild. Pessa. Lyssa. Jorren. Work if it appeared. Theatre again when they came back, assuming they came back when expected. Nothing required me to leave Carrow. That was important. I was not being forced onto a road. I was not fleeing anything.

I was not chasing work I needed to survive. I was not even formally part of the troupe. There were excellent reasons not to go.

"Hessa."

She turned.

"If I travel tomorrow, is today the last assessment before I leave?"

"Yes."

I nodded.

"That is irritating."

"Yes."

She came back to the table and pushed the newer drawing toward me.

"What?"

"Take it."

I stared.

"You keep the records."

"I have the record."

She tapped her ledger.

"Take the drawing."

"Why?"

"So when you spend six days thinking about it, you can at least think about the thing you actually reported."

I picked it up.

"That sounds like permission to analyze it."

"No magic."

"I said analyze."

"No reconstructing the sensation."

"I can't promise not to remember my own arm."

"You know the difference."

I did. Mostly. I folded the paper once. Hessa immediately said, "Don't." I unfolded it.

"Why?"

"You just folded through the wrist boundary."

I stared at her.

"You said the drawing isn't independent evidence."

"It isn't."

"Then why does the fold matter?"

"Because now I have to wonder whether you will later remember the fold as part of the line."

I looked at the charcoal mark. Then at her.

"That is extremely annoying."

"Yes."

She gave me a scrap of stiff paper to carry it between. I slid the drawing inside. At the door I collected my crutches.

"Hessa."

"What?"

"If I go east, and nothing changes, I come back and we continue?"

"Yes."

"Same restrictions."

"Yes."

"Same question?"

"We'll see."

I opened the door.

"And Gregory?"

I looked back. She had already reopened the ledger.

"What?"

"Go because you want to go."

I frowned.

"I told you. The municipal hall."

"Yes."

"The roof is genuinely interesting."

"I believe you."

"And I'm useful to the theatre."

"I didn't ask."

"They need the sword."

"Gregory."

"And possibly the Shopkeeper."

"Leave my office."

I did. The street outside was brighter than I expected. A produce cart blocked half the lane, and two women were arguing over whether a basket of onions belonged to one of them or to a shop three doors down. Someone had hung wet shirts from an upper window. They snapped in the breeze above the street like surrender flags nobody respected. I tucked Hessa's drawing safely inside my coat. The theatre left tomorrow. I had an entire day to decide whether I was going. I turned west.
CHAPTER 140
THE TRAVELER

I turned west because Lyssa was usually west in the morning. That was not the same as going to find her. It was merely using information I already possessed while traveling through the city. This distinction survived for almost three streets. Then I passed a bakery I did not need, ignored the guild road entirely, and asked a woman unloading blue cloth whether she had seen Lyssa. Fine. I was going to find her. The woman pointed with her chin.

"South square."

"That is not west."

"She moved."

"I know people can move."

The woman looked at my crutches. I looked at her. She went back to the cloth. Carrow was warm already. The night damp had burned off the stones, leaving the streets bright and dusty wherever wagon wheels had ground dirt into the gaps. A fish seller was throwing water across his boards. Two apprentices carried a door between them without looking where they were going. I moved. The door missed me. Barely. One apprentice said, "Sorry." The other said, "You were in the way."

I considered following them to explain geometry. I had other work. Not work. Something else. Lyssa was in the south square beside a stack of baskets, talking to an older woman with silver rings on three fingers. The woman held a folded length of green cloth. Lyssa held the other end. Neither looked happy. Good. Normal. I stopped outside the argument. Lyssa saw me first. Her eyes went to my coat, then my face.

"Hessa?"

"Done."

The older woman looked at me.

"Who is that?"

"Gregory."

"That explains nothing."

"It usually doesn't," Lyssa said.

I disliked how easily that came to her. The woman tugged the cloth. Lyssa did not let go.

"It was dry when I gave it to him."

"It is wet now."

"Then he got it wet."

"He says you gave it to him wet."

"He lies."

"He says you lie."

"Then he lies twice."

I looked at the cloth. One end was damp. Not soaked. Damp.

"What happened?"

Both women looked at me. Lyssa said, "No."

"I only asked."

The older woman handed Lyssa the cloth abruptly.

"Half."

"No."

"Then take it back."

"I don't want wet cloth."

"You brought me wet cloth."

"I brought you dry cloth."

"You just said you didn't bring it."

"I said he brought it."

The woman pointed somewhere behind me. A boy was standing near a fountain trying very hard to become architecture. Ah. I looked at him. He looked away. Lyssa followed my eyes.

"Leave him," she said.

"I only looked."

"Yes." This was becoming unreasonable. Lyssa finally let go of the cloth.

"Half now. Other half when it dries clean."

The woman considered.

"Quarter now."

"Half."

"Third."

"Half."

"You are bad at bargaining."

"You keep moving toward me."

The woman stared at her. Then laughed once.

"Fine."

Money changed hands. The boy near the fountain vanished. Lyssa folded the damp cloth over her arm. I watched.

"What?" she asked.

"You accepted the cloth."

"Yes."

"You said you didn't want it."

"I don't."

"You're carrying it."

"Gregory."

"Fine."

She turned to the older woman.

"Tomorrow?"

"Not with him."

Lyssa looked toward the fountain.

"No."

The woman left. Lyssa stood with wet green cloth over one arm and her work bag over the other shoulder. The ugly black repair still held. I had been right that it would. It remained ugly. She looked at me.

"Well?"

"Well what?"

"Hessa."

"Oh."

"You came over and said done like you finished breakfast."

"It was not breakfast."

"I know."

"Nothing happened."

Lyssa waited. I corrected myself.

"Nothing external happened."

"Good?"

"Unclear."

She smiled.

"Fuck you."

"You said it."

"It is becoming contagious."

We started walking without discussing where. I fell into the position beside her that kept my right crutch away from her feet. She had learned it too. She shifted the wet cloth to her other arm without looking.

"The neutral shape may not be neutral," I said.

Lyssa glanced at me.

"Those words sound like they are fighting."

"It is a label."

"For something that isn't what the label says?"

"Possibly."

"Good label."

"Hessa would like you."

"No."

"No?"

"She tells you not to do magic."

"Yes."

"I tell you not to do magic."

"Sometimes."

"When Hessa tells you."

"Exactly."

Lyssa bumped my shoulder with hers. Light.

"Continue."

I explained the wrist-side boundary. Not all of it. Enough. The two drawings. The repeated asymmetry. The problem with comparing the directional tests to a baseline we had not described well enough before testing direction. Lyssa listened while watching the street. That was one of the differences between her and Hessa. Hessa listened like she was building a cage around the answer. Lyssa listened like the answer could walk beside her if it wanted.

"So the old test might still mean something," she said.

"Yes."

"But less."

"Yes."

"And you hate that."

"Yes."

"Good."

I stopped. She kept walking two steps, then looked back.

"Why is that good?"

"Because last time you liked maybe too much."

"I did not."

"You did."

"I respected the evidence."

"You were excited."

"That is allowed."

"Yes."

"Then why are you saying it like a diagnosis?"

She smiled.

"Come on."

I caught up. We turned into a narrower street where awnings nearly met overhead. The shade was cooler. A cooper had barrels lined along one wall, forcing everyone into a single crooked path around them. Lyssa went first. I followed, planting the crutches carefully between iron hoops and people's feet. A man came the other way carrying three long poles. He turned sideways. So did I. Wrong choice. One pole caught my left crutch near the cuff. I stopped. The man stopped. Lyssa turned. Nobody moved.

The pole man said, "Well."

"Yes," I said.

Lyssa took the outer pole and lifted it over my shoulder.

"Go."

He went. I looked at her.

"You solved it."

"Yes."

"I had it."

"No."

"I was about to."

"You were attached to a pole."

"Temporarily."

She kept walking. I followed. This was why travel with other people was useful. Not that I was traveling. Yet. I had not decided. The theatre left tomorrow. Hessa had not objected. That was not permission because permission was not hers to give. The municipal hall remained structurally interesting. The troupe had explicitly stated that other towns contained chairs. There were several variables. Lyssa stopped at a doorway and knocked. I nearly continued past her.

"What?"

"Work."

"Oh."

A young man opened the door. He saw Lyssa. Then me.

"No."

I looked at him. Lyssa said, "He's not coming in."

"Good."

"What is inside?"

"Gregory."

"I am asking spatially."

The young man looked at Lyssa.

"Does he do this?"

"Yes."

"Constantly?"

"Not constantly."

"Frequently."

"Thank you."

Lyssa handed him the folded wet cloth. He frowned.

"This is wet."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Because everyone is difficult."

He accepted that. Apparently this was a professional category. Lyssa took a small packet from her bag and gave it to him. He gave her another. Then he looked at me again.

"Landlord?"

"No."

Lyssa said, "Shopkeeper now." I turned.

"What?"

The young man smiled.

"Oh. That was you?"

No. Absolutely not.

"How do you know?"

"My sister was there."

"At the market hall?"

"Yes."

"What did she say?"

Lyssa leaned against the doorframe. The young man thought.

"That the king was terrible."

Correct.

"And?"

"The princess was good."

Correct.

"And?"

"The man with one foot threatened somebody about debt."

"That was not a threat."

He laughed.

"She said it was."

"It was consultation."

That made him laugh harder. Lyssa looked delighted. I hated public performance.

"Did she say anything about the sword?"

"The talking one?"

"Yes."

He shrugged.

"Funny."

"That is all?"

"What else would it be?"

I opened my mouth. Closed it. Fair. The young man shut the door. Lyssa waited. I started walking. She caught up.

"Funny."

"Stop."

"The talking one."

"Lyssa."

"Shopkeeper."

"That is not my name."

"It was last night."

"No."

She laughed. I let her. For three streets. Then she said, "You're going." I looked at her.

"Where?"

She did not answer. That was irritating.

"I have not decided."

"You came to find me after Hessa."

"I have done that before."

"Yes."

"I wanted to see you."

"I know."

"And I needed to tell you."

She looked at me. There. That had escaped. Fine.

"Tell me what?" she asked.

"The theatre leaves tomorrow."

Her face changed only slightly. Not fear. Not surprise exactly. Attention.

"How long?"

"Five days. Maybe six."

"Where?"

I told her. She knew the road but not the town.

"Why?"

"Theatre."

"I got that."

"There is also a municipal hall."

Lyssa stared at me.

"What?"

"You're leaving for a building?"

"The roof was rebuilt twice."

She kept staring.

"The original load paths are strange."

"Gregory."

"I wanted to see it years ago."

"How many years?"

I stopped. Ah.

"Many."

She understood. Not everything. Enough. The street moved around us. A woman squeezed past carrying a basket of onions. Somewhere behind us, a hammer struck metal in a steady rhythm. Lyssa stepped closer to the wall so we were not blocking the lane.

"And the theatre happens to be going there."

"Yes."

"Tomorrow."

"Yes."

"For five days."

"Maybe six."

"You're going."

"I said I haven't decided."

She reached out and straightened the edge of my coat where Hessa's stiff paper had made it bulge.

"You put the drawing in here."

"Yes."

"You came straight to find me."

"Mostly."

"You asked someone where I was."

"Yes."

"You're telling me before you told me you've decided."

"I have not decided."

Lyssa nodded.

"Fine."

That was too easy.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"No."

She started walking again. I followed.

"You're doing the thing."

"What thing?"

"Where you stop arguing because you think you already know."

"I don't know."

"You do."

"No."

"Lyssa."

She turned into the next square. I followed, irritated enough that I almost clipped a fruit crate.

"Lyssa."

She stopped beside a fountain. Not the pigeon fountain. Good.

"What do you want me to say?"

"I don't know."

"Then why are you angry?"

"I am not angry."

"You're hitting the ground harder."

I looked at my right crutch. Traitor.

"I am explaining that the decision is not made."

"Okay."

"You don't believe me."

"I believe you haven't said it."

"That is different."

"Yes."

I waited. She waited. People crossed between us and the fountain. A little boy leaned over the basin until his mother pulled him backward by his shirt.

"Do you want me to tell you not to go?" Lyssa asked.

"No."

"Do you want me to tell you to go?"

"No."

"Do you want me to be upset?"

I frowned.

"No."

She looked at me for another second.

Then softer:

"Do you want me to care?"

That was a much worse question.

"I know you care."

"Then?"

I looked away. A horse was drinking from the far side of the fountain. Its driver held the reins loosely and picked something from his teeth. Five days. Maybe six. Not long. I had traveled farther for worse reasons. I had also died. Different trip.

"I wanted to tell you," I said.

"I know."

"Before."

"I know."

"I don't know what you're doing tomorrow."

"Work."

"Obviously."

"Morning north side. Afternoon maybe west."

"Maybe?"

She smiled.

"Contagious."

I ignored that.

"I leave early if I go."

"If."

"Yes."

"Fine."

I looked at her. She did not rescue me. Good. Annoying.

"Could I see you tonight?"

"Yes."

Immediate. No bargaining. Something in my chest loosened enough that I noticed it.

"Where?"

"My room."

I blinked. Lyssa raised an eyebrow.

"You've been there."

"Yes."

"You look surprised."

"I am not."

"You are."

"I was calculating stairs."

"No, you weren't."

I smiled despite myself.

"Some."

"Liar."

"Fine."

She stepped close and kissed me. Not long. Public enough that a woman passing with a basket looked at us and then politely looked somewhere else. Lyssa drew back.

"Go tell your theatre."

"I haven't decided."

"Then go inspect the wagon for six hours until the decision becomes official."

"That is insulting."

"Will you?"

I thought about the south-road wheels. The loading. How much weight I could actually move. Whether there was space to ride if my hands got bad. Where the crutches would go. What happened if the town had stairs everywhere. Whether Teren had assumed I was coming or merely offered. Whether the servant actor could throw his voice from a moving wagon. No. That last one was irrelevant. Probably.

"I should ask about the road."

Lyssa nodded.

"And the wagon."

"Yes."

"And sleeping arrangements."

"Yes."

"And whether they expect me to carry anything."

"Yes."

"And how many shows."

"Yes."

"That is not the same as deciding."

"No."

She was smiling.

"Stop."

"I didn't say anything."

"You're doing it with your face."

"I have one face."

"That is my line."

"It is everyone's line now."

She kissed me again. Then she stepped away and adjusted her work bag.

"I have to go."

"Where?"

"North."

"You said morning north."

"It is still morning."

I looked at the sun. Barely.

"That assessment took longer than I thought."

"You talked."

"Hessa talks."

"Sure."

"She does."

Lyssa started backward for two steps.

"Tonight."

"Yes."

"Don't arrive after I'm asleep."

"What time?"

She gave me a look. Right. Not everything required measurement.

"Before late."

"Good."

She turned.

"Lyssa."

She looked back. I nearly said I was going. The words were there. Instead I said, "The black patch is still ugly." She looked down at her bag. Then at me.

"Five days might improve your taste."

"Six would not."

She laughed and walked away. I watched longer than two seconds this time. She did not turn around. Good. I headed for the theatre. Not because I had decided. I needed information. The theatre doors were open when I arrived. A flat painted like a stone tower was halfway into the alley, blocking most of it. The soot-shirt worker stood on the wagon bed with a coil of rope around his neck, shouting at someone inside.

"Not that one. The other ugly one."

A voice answered, "They're both ugly."

"The tall ugly one."

"That is not better."

I stopped beside the wagon. One rear wheel had been removed. Good. South-road wheels. The servant actor was underneath it. I could see his boots.

"Teren?"

"Inside," the soot-shirt worker said.

"Why is the wheel off?"

The boots under the wagon moved.

"Because it was bad."

"How bad?"

The servant actor slid out on his back. His shirt was dusty and his hair had something black in it.

"Bad enough."

"That is not a measurement."

"It is for wheels."

He sat up.

"You coming?"

I looked at the missing wheel.

"I have questions."

He smiled.

"Coming."

"Questions."

"Ask."

"How long on the road tomorrow?"

"Depends."

"On?"

"Road."

I stared at him. He wiped his hands on his trousers.

"Three hours to first stop if the axle behaves. Eat. Another three, maybe four. We sleep there."

"Where?"

He named a village I knew.

"Then?"

"Shorter second day."

"That makes the trip longer than five days."

"Five or six there and back if nothing goes wrong."

"That is impossible."

"Then six."

"Teren said five maybe six."

"He lies optimistically."

Useful.

"Sleeping?"

"Inns if rooms exist. Hall floor if they don't. Wagon once, probably."

"Probably?"

"Gregory."

"What?"

"You are asking theatre people for certainty."

Fair.

"Shows?"

"Two planned. Maybe three."

"Shopkeeper?"

"If Meren remains dead."

"He isn't dead."

"Then he should arrive."

"Do I have a role if he does?"

The servant actor looked at me.

"Sword."

"Yes."

"And whatever breaks."

"That is not a role."

"It is the oldest role."

The soot-shirt worker shouted from the wagon, "Can the oldest role lift a wheel?"

"No," I said.

"Then he's decorative."

"Fuck you."

"See? Actor."

The servant actor laughed. I looked at the wagon bed.

"Where do I sit?"

He pointed.

"Front if Teren loses the argument. Back if he wins."

"What argument?"

"Seats."

"With whom?"

"The wagon owner."

"Why?"

"Wagon owner wants cargo where people go."

"That seems backwards."

"Yes."

"Can I secure crutches?"

"We'll tie them."

"Where?"

He pointed to a rail. I inspected it. Solid enough. Probably.

"And if my hands get bad?"

"You ride."

"I am already riding."

"You ride more."

"I mean during loading."

"Then don't load."

"That makes me a hindrance."

He looked at me. Not joking now.

"No. It makes you a man who doesn't load."

"I can carry some things."

"Then carry some things."

"And when I can't?"

"Don't."

"That is not efficient."

He shrugged.

"We have actors."

"That does not answer anything."

"It answers most things."

From inside, Teren shouted, "Sword!" I looked toward the door. The servant actor grinned.

"See?"

I went in. Teren was at a table covered in pages, receipts, two apples, a broken buckle, and a small pile of coins. He did not look up.

"You're coming."

"I have questions."

"Tomorrow before sunrise."

"That is not a question."

"Bring food."

"I haven't said yes."

"Bring food anyway."

"How many shows?"

"Two."

"He said maybe three."

Teren looked toward the alley.

"Who?"

"The king."

"Never trust kings."

"He said you lie optimistically."

Teren considered.

"Fair."

I put both hands on the table edge.

"Where am I sleeping?"

"Wherever we all sleep."

"That is not useful."

"No."

"Do you know whether the municipal hall has stairs to the stage?"

Teren finally looked at me.

"No."

"Back entrance?"

"No."

"Dressing rooms?"

"No."

"Floor height?"

"No."

"Chair?"

"Yes."

"You don't know the rest."

"I know chairs."

"How?"

"Town has people."

I stared. The troupe's faith in chairs was becoming theological. Teren picked up an apple.

"Gregory."

"What?"

"Are you coming?"

I looked at the pages. The receipts. The broken buckle. The coins. Outside, someone hammered the wheel back into existence. Tonight I was going to Lyssa's room. Tomorrow before sunrise the wagon left east. Hessa's drawing sat inside my coat. There were no good reasons left to pretend the decision required another category.

"Yes," I said.

Teren bit into the apple.

"Good. Bring food."

That was all. No welcome. No contract. No speech about the road. He pushed a packet of pages toward me.

"What is this?"

"Third show."

I stared at him.

"You said two."

"Maybe three."

"Fuck you."

"Learn page twelve."

I took the packet. Apparently I was traveling.
